then
\mathscr{I}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}\mathcalx{F}(u\>{\mathsf{diff}}{\langle\tau,\upsilon\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(s,t))\approx\mathcalx{F}(w\>{\mathsf{diff}}{\langle\tau,\upsilon\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(s,t))
.

As another building block of our redundancy criterion,
we introduce the notion of trust.
As a motivating example, consider the clauses

{\mathsf{b}}\not\approx{\mathsf{a}}
and

{\mathsf{b}}\approx{\mathsf{a}}
, where
{\mathsf{b}}\succ{\mathsf{a}}
.
Clearly, the empty clause can be derived via a
Sup
and a
EqRes
inference.
If we replace the clause
{\mathsf{b}}\approx{\mathsf{a}}
with
the logically equivalent clause
x\not\approx{\mathsf{a}}\>[\![x\equiv{\mathsf{b}}]\!]
, however,
an empty clause with satisfiable constraints cannot be derived because
Sup
does not apply at variables.
In this sense, the clause
{\mathsf{b}}\not\approx{\mathsf{a}}

is more powerful than
x\not\approx{\mathsf{a}}\>[\![x\equiv{\mathsf{b}}]\!]
.
Technically,
the reason for this is that
the calculus is only guaranteed to derive contradictions entailed by
so-called variable-irreducible instances
of clauses,
and the instance of
x\not\approx{\mathsf{a}}\>[\![x\equiv{\mathsf{b}}]\!]
that maps

x
to
{\mathsf{b}}
is not variable-irreducible.
Since variable-irreducibility cannot be computed in general,
when we replace a clause with another,
we use the notion of trust to ensure that
for every variable-irreducible instance of the replaced clause,
there exists a corresponding variable-irreducible instance of the replacing clause.
Concretely,
for any variable that occurs in a constraint or in a parameter of the replacing clause,
there must exist a variable in a similar context in the replaced clause.
The formal definition is as follows.

{defi}

[Trust]
Let
C\theta
be a ground instance of
C[\![S]\!]\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}

and
D\rho
be a ground instance of
D[\![T]\!]\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
We say that the
\theta
-instance of
C[\![S]\!]

trusts
the
\rho
-instance of
D[\![T]\!]

if for each variable
x
in
D
,

(i)

for every literal
L\in D

containing
x
outside of parameters,
there exists a literal
K\in C
and a substitution
\sigma
such that

z\theta=z\sigma\rho
for all variables
z
in
C

and
L\preceq K\sigma
; or

(ii)

x
neither occurs in parameters in
D
nor appears in
T
.

The most general form of redundancy criteria for constrained superposition calculi
are notoriously difficult to apply to concrete simplification rules.
In the spirit of Nieuwenhuis and Rubio
[
23
]
, we therefore
introduce a simpler, less general notion of redundancy that suffices for most simplification rules.
We provide a simple criterion for clauses and one for inference rules.

6.2.1.
Simple Clause Redundancy

Our redundancy criterion for clauses provides two conditions that can make a clause redundant.
The first condition applies when the ground instances of a clause are entailed
by smaller ground instances of other clauses.
It generalizes the standard superposition redundancy criterion
to higher-order clauses with constraints.
The second condition applies when there are other clauses with the same ground instances
and can be used to justify subsumption.
For this second condition, we fix a well-founded partial order

\sqsupset
on
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
,
which prevents infinite chains of clauses where each clause is made redundant by the next one.

{defi}

[Simple Clause Redundancy]
Let
N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
and
C[\![S]\!]\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
We call
C[\![S]\!]

simply redundant

w.r.t.

N
, written
C[\![S]\!]\in{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{C}}^{\star}(N)
,
if for every
C\theta\in{\mathsf{Gnd}}(C[\![S]\!])

at least one of the following two conditions holds:

1.

There exist
an indexing set
I
and for each
i\in I

a ground instance
D_{i}\rho_{i}
of a clause

D_{i}[\![T_{i}]\!]\in N
,
such that

(a)

\mathcalx{F}(\{D_{i}\rho_{i}\mid i\in I\})\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathcalx{F}(C\theta)
;

(b)

for all
i\in I
,
D_{i}\rho_{i}\prec C\theta
; and

(c)

for all
i\in I
, the
\theta
-instance of
C[\![S]\!]
trusts the
\rho_{i}
-instance
of
D_{i}[\![T_{i}]\!]
.

2.

There exists a
ground instance
D\rho
of some

D[\![T]\!]\in N

such that

(a)

D\rho=C\theta
;

(b)

C[\![S]\!]\sqsupset D[\![T]\!]
; and

(c)

the
\theta
-instance of
C[\![S]\!]
trusts the
\rho
-instance
of
D[\![T]\!]
.

Remark 8
.

Although the calculus is refutationally complete for any choice of
\sqsupset
,
we propose the following definition for
\sqsupset
.
Given a clause
C[\![S]\!]
with nonempty
S
and a clause
D
with no constraints,
we define
C[\![S]\!]\sqsupset D
.
For two clauses
C
and
D
with no constraints, following Bentkamp et al.
[
8
,

7.

3.4]

, we propose to define
C\sqsupset D

if either
C
is larger than
D
in syntactic size (i.e., number of variables, constants, and De Bruijn indices),
or if
C
and
D
have the same syntactic size and
C
contains fewer distinct variables than
D
.

7.0.1.
Simple Inference Redundancy

To define inference redundancy,
we first define a calculus
\mathit{FInf}

on ground first-order logic with Booleans.
It is parameterized by a relation
\succ
on
ground first-order terms.

For simplicity, there is no selection function,
but our notion
of eligibility is adapted to overapproximate any possible selection function as follows.
A literal
L\in C
is (
strictly
)
eligible
in
C
if
L
is
negative
or if
L
is of the form
t\approx\kern 0.17224pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern 0.17224pt

or if
L
is (strictly) maximal in
C
.
A position

L.s.p

of a clause
C
is
eligible

if the literal
L
is
of the form
s\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}t
with
s\succ t

and
L
is either
negative and
eligible
or positive and strictly eligible.

Every term is a green subterm of itself.
Every direct subterm of a nonfunctional green subterm is also a green subterm.

{defi}

Since
\mathcalx{F}
is bijective on ground terms by Lemma
7
,
we can convert a term order
\succ
on higher-order terms
into a relation
\succ{F}
on ground first-order terms as follows.
For two ground first-order terms
s
and
t
, let
s\mathrel{\succ{F}}t
if
\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(s)\succ\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(t)
.

{defi}

Let
\iota\in\mathit{HInf}^{\succ,\mathit{hsel}}

for a term order
\succ
and a selection function
\mathit{hsel}
.
Let
C_{1}[\![S_{1}]\!]
, …,
C_{m}[\![S_{m}]\!]
be its premises and

C_{m+1}[\![S_{m+1}]\!]
its conclusion.
Let
(\theta_{1}
, …,
\theta_{m+1})
be a tuple of grounding substitutions.
We say that
\iota
is
rooted
in
\mathit{FInf}{}
for
(\theta_{1}
, …,
\theta_{m+1})

if and only if

–

S_{1}\theta_{1},\dots,S_{m+1}\theta_{m+1}
are true
and

–

\displaystyle{\mathcalx{F}(C_{1}\theta_{1})\quad\cdots\quad\mathcalx{F}(C_{m}\theta_{m})}\mathstrut

\displaystyle\mathcalx{F}(C_{m+1}\theta_{m+1})\mathstrut

is a valid
\mathit{FInf}^{\succ{F}}
inference
\iota^{\prime}

such that the rule names of
\iota
and
\iota^{\prime}
correspond up to the prefixes
F
and
Fluid
.

{defi}

[Simple Inference Redundancy]
Let
N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
Let
\iota\in\mathit{HInf}

an inference with premises
C_{1}[\![S_{1}]\!]
, …,
C_{m}[\![S_{m}]\!]
and
conclusion
C_{m+1}[\![S_{m+1}]\!]
.
We call
\iota

simply redundant

w.r.t.

N
, written
\iota\in{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\star}(N)
,
if for every tuple of substitutions
(\theta_{1}
, …,
\theta_{m+1})

for which
\iota
is rooted in
\mathit{FInf}
(Definition
7.0.1
),
there exists an index set
I
and
for each
i\in I
a ground instance
D_{i}\rho_{i}
of a clause

D_{i}[\![T_{i}]\!]\in N

such that

1.

\mathcalx{F}(\{D_{i}\rho_{i}\mid i\in I\})\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathcalx{F}(C_{m+1}\theta_{m+1})
;

2.

\iota
is a
Diff
inference or for all
i\in I
,
D_{i}\rho_{i}\prec C_{m}\theta_{m}
; and

3.

for all
i\in I
, the
\theta_{m+1}
-instance of
C_{m+1}[\![S_{m+1}]\!]
trusts the
\rho_{i}
-instance
of
D_{i}[\![T_{i}]\!]
.

7.1.
Simplification Rules

7.1.1.
Analogues of First-Order Simplification Rules

Our notion of simple clause redundancy (Definition
6.2.1
)
can justify most analogues of the
simplification rules implemented in Schulz’s E prover
[
27
, Sections
2.3.1 and 2.3.2]
. Deletion of duplicated literals,
deletion of resolved literals, and syntactic tautology deletion
adhere to our redundancy criterion, even when the involved clauses carry constraints.
Semantic tautology deletion can be applied as
well, even on constrained clauses, but we must use the entailment relation
\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}
under the encoding
\mathcalx{F}
.

Positive and negative simplify-reflect can be applied as well, even with constraints,
as long as the substitution makes each constraint of the unit clause true
or translates it into a constraint already present on the other clause.

Our analogue of clause subsumption is the following.
The subsumed clause can have constraints, but the subsuming clause cannot.

\displaystyle{C\quad C\sigma\mathrel{\lor}D\>[\![S]\!]}\mathstrut

Subsumption

\displaystyle C\mathstrut

with the following side conditions:

1.

D\neq\bot
or
C\sigma[\![S]\!]\sqsupset C
;

2.

C
does not contain a variable occurring both inside and outside of parameters.

Lemma 9
.

Subsumption
can be justified by simple clause redundancy.

Proof 7.1
.

Let
(C\sigma\mathrel{\lor}D)\theta\in{\mathsf{Gnd}}(C\sigma\mathrel{\lor}D[\![S]\!])
.

If
D
is nonempty, we apply condition
1

of Definition
6.2.1
,
using
I=\{*\}
,
D_{*}=C
and
\rho_{*}=\sigma\theta
.
The clause
C\sigma\theta
is a proper subclause of

(C\sigma\mathrel{\lor}D)\theta

and therefore

\mathcalx{F}(C\sigma\theta)\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathcalx{F}((C\sigma\mathrel{\lor}D)\theta)

(condition
1a
)
and
C\sigma\theta\prec(C\sigma\mathrel{\lor}D)\theta

(condition
1b
).
For condition
1c
,
let
x
be a variable in
C
.
By condition
2
of
Subsumption
,

x
occurs only inside parameters or only outside parameters.
If it occurs only inside, we apply condition
(i)

of Definition
6.2
;
if it occurs only outside, we apply condition
(ii)

of Definition
6.2
.

If
D
is
\bot
, we apply condition
2
of Definition
6.2.1
,
using
C
for
D
and
\sigma\theta
for
\rho

Condition
2a

clearly holds.
Condition
2b
holds by condition
1

of
Subsumption
.
Condition

follows from condition
2

of
Subsumption
as above.

Remark 12
.

In general, it is unclear how to compute condition
3
of
Demod
.
For
\lambda
KBO and
\lambda
LPO described in Section
5.1
,
however, the condition can easily be overapproximated by

C\begin{picture}\put(1.1,2.5){\rotatebox{45.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\put(1.1,2.5){\rotatebox{315.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\end{picture}\!\!\begin{picture}\put(1.1,2.5){\rotatebox{45.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\put(1.1,2.5){\rotatebox{315.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\end{picture}\,v\begin{picture}\put(0.0,2.5){\rotatebox{135.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\put(0.0,2.5){\rotatebox{225.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\end{picture}\!\!\begin{picture}\put(0.0,2.5){\rotatebox{135.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\put(0.0,2.5){\rotatebox{225.0}{\line{1}{0}{6.0}}}\end{picture}\succ v\approx v^{\prime}
,
using the fact that the orders are also defined on preterms.

To prove that this is a valid overapproximation, it suffices to show the following:
Let
u
and
s
be preterms with
u\succ s
(resp.
u\succsim s
). Let
s^{\prime}
be the result of replacing some De Bruijn indices in
s
by
terms of the form
{\mathsf{diff}}{\langle\_,\_\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(\_,\_)
. Then
u\succ s^{\prime}
(resp.
u\succsim s^{\prime}
).

Proof for
\lambda
KBO:
By induction on the rule deriving
u\succ s
or
u\succsim s
.
Since we assume in Section
5.1
that

\cal w_{\mathsf{db}}\geq\cal w({\mathsf{diff}})
and
\cal k({\mathsf{diff}},i)=1
for every
i
,
we have
\cal W(s)\geq\cal W(s^{\prime})
.
It is easy to check that there is always a corresponding rule deriving
u\succ s^{\prime}
or
u\succsim s^{\prime}
,
in some cases using the induction hypothesis.

Proof for
\lambda
LPO:
By induction on the rule deriving
u\succ s
or
u\succsim s
.
Considering that we assume in Section

For each of these clauses, we can again apply a

inference using (1), (2), or (3), in two different ways each.
After applying

to their conclusions, we obtain three more clauses:

So, without literal selection, depending on the prover’s heuristics, a prover might in the worst case need to perform
3+3\cdot 2+1=10

Sup
inferences
to derive the empty clause.

Now, let us consider the same initial clause set but we select exactly one literal whenever possible.
In (4), we can select one of the literals, say the first one. Then there is only one possible

inference:
(1) into (4), yielding (5) after applying
FalseElim
. In (5), we can again select the first literal.
Again, only one

inference is possible, yielding

{\mathsf{r}}\>z\approx\kern 0.17224pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern 0.17224pt
after applying
FalseElim
.
Another
Sup
and another
FalseElim
inference yield the empty clause.
Overall, there is a unique derivation of the empty clause, consisting of only three
Sup
inferences.

{exa}

[Simplification of Functional Literals]
Consider the following clauses, where
{\mathsf{f}}
and
{\mathsf{g}}
are constants of type
\iota\to\iota
.

\displaystyle(1)\ {\mathsf{f}}\approx{\mathsf{g}}

\displaystyle(2)\ {\mathsf{f}}\not\approx{\mathsf{g}}

A
Sup
inference from (1) into (2) is not possible because the terms are functional.
Instead, we can apply
ArgCong
and
NegExt
to derive the following clauses:

\displaystyle(3)\ {\mathsf{f}}\>x\approx{\mathsf{g}}\>x\text{\quad(by $\textsc{Arg\-Cong}$ from (1))}

\displaystyle(4)\ {\mathsf{f}}\>{\mathsf{diff}}({\mathsf{f}},{\mathsf{g}})\not\approx{\mathsf{g}}\>{\mathsf{diff}}({\mathsf{f}},{\mathsf{g}})\text{\quad(by $\textsc{NegExt}$ from (2))}

Both
ArgCong
and
NegExt
are simplification rules,
so we can delete (1) and (2) after deriving (3) and (4).
Now, a
Sup
inference from (3) into (4) and a
EqRes
inference yield the empty clause.

In contrast, the original superposition calculus requires both the
Sup
inference from (1) into (2)
and also a derivation similar to the one above. Moreover, its redundancy criterion
does not allow us to delete (1) and (2). This amounts to doubling the number of clauses and
inferences—even more if
{\mathsf{f}}
and
{\mathsf{g}}
had more than one argument.

{exa}

[Extensionality Reasoning]
Consider the following clauses:

\displaystyle(1)\ {\mathsf{map}}\>(\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1))\>x\not\approx{\mathsf{map}}\>(\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>u))\>x

\displaystyle(2)\ {\mathsf{add}}\>u\>v\approx{\mathsf{add}}\>v\>u

For better readability, we omit type arguments and use subscripts for the parameters of
{\mathsf{diff}}
.
Using our calculus, we derive the following clauses:

\displaystyle(3)\ {\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>({\mathsf{diff}}_{\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1),z})\>1)\not\approx z\>({\mathsf{diff}}_{\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1),z})\mathrel{\lor}

\displaystyle\phantom{(0)\ }{\mathsf{map}}\>z\>x\not\approx{\mathsf{map}}\>(\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>u))\>x\text{\quad(by $\textsc{Ext}$ from (1))}

\displaystyle(4)\ {\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1),\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>u)}\>1)\not\approx

\displaystyle\phantom{(0)\ }{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1),\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>u)})\text{\quad(by $\textsc{EqRes}$ from (3))}

\displaystyle(5)\ {\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1),\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>u)})\not\approx

\displaystyle\phantom{(0)\ }{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>u\>1),\lambda u.\>{\mathsf{sqrt}}\>({\mathsf{add}}\>1\>u)})\text{\quad(by $\textsc{Sup}$ from (2), (4))}

\displaystyle(6)\ \bot\text{\quad(by $\textsc{EqRes}$ from (5))}

While such a derivation is also possible in the original
\lambda
-superposition calculus,
the term orders of the original calculus were not able to compare
the literals of the extensionality axiom

y\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{y,z}\not\approx z\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{y,z}\mathrel{\lor}y\approx z

As a result, the extensionality axiom leads to an explosion of inferences.
Our calculus avoids this problem by ensuring that the positive literal of
the extensionality axiom is maximal, via the ordering property
(O5)
.
By replacing the extensionality axiom with the
Ext
rule,
we avoid in addition
Sup
inferences into functional terms,
and it strengthens our redundancy criterion.

{exa}

If our calculus did not support constraints, we would have to solve the unification problem in (3) first,
which yields an infinite number of solutions among which the simplest ones are dead ends.

Assuming that the negative literal in (7) is selected
and that
{\mathsf{b}}\succ{\mathsf{a}}
,
no core inference rule other than
Diff
applies.
Due to the explosive nature of
Diff
,
it is difficult to predict whether
Diff
inferences lead anywhere,
but we conjecture that this is indeed a counterexample
to a redundancy criterion that ignores parameters.

An alternative approach with a stronger redundancy criterion
that does not need to treat parameters specially
may be to enforce superposition inferences into
variables that have other occurrences inside parameters.
In the example above, this would entail a superposition inference
from (1) into the variable
y
in the second literal of (7),
which would indeed lead to a refutation.

8.
Soundness

To prove our calculus sound, we need a substitution lemma for terms and clauses,
which our logic fulfills:

Lemma 22

(Substitution Lemma)
.

Let
\theta
be a substitution, and let
t
be a term of type
\tau
.
For any proper interpretation
\mathscr{I}=(\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}},\mathscr{J},\mathscr{L})
and any valuation
\xi
,

\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}=\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}

where the modified valuation
\xi^{\prime}
is defined
by
\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime}(\alpha)=\smash{\llbracket\alpha\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}}}

for type variables
\alpha

and
\xi_{\mathsf{te}}^{\prime}(x)=\smash{\llbracket x\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}
for term variables
x
.

Proof 8.1
.

By induction on the size of the term
t
.

Case

t=x\langle\tau\rangle
:

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket x\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\xi^{\prime}(x)\quad\text{(by the definition of interpretation)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket x\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}\quad\text{(since $x$ is mapped to $\smash{\llbracket x\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}$)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}

Case

t={\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}{(\bar{u})}
:

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\theta\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}{(\bar{u}\theta)}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\mathscr{J}\left({\mathsf{f}},\smash{\llbracket\bar{\tau}\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}}},\smash{\llbracket\bar{u}\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}\right)\quad\text{(by definition)}

\displaystyle=\mathscr{J}\left({\mathsf{f}},\smash{\llbracket\bar{\tau}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime}}},\smash{\llbracket\bar{u}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}\right)\quad\text{(by induction hypothesis)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}{(\bar{u})}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}\quad\text{(by definition)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}

Case

t=s\>v
:

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket s\theta\>v\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket s\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}\left(\smash{\llbracket v\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}\right)\quad\text{(by definition)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}\left(\smash{\llbracket v\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}\right)\quad\text{(by induction hypothesis)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket s\>v\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}\quad\text{(by definition)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}

Case

t=\lambda\langle\tau\rangle\>u
:

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}(a)

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket\lambda\langle\tau\theta\rangle\>u\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}(a)

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket u\theta\{0\mapsto x\}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}}[x\mapsto a])}}\quad\text{(since $\mathscr{I}$ is proper; for some fresh variable $x$)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket u\{0\mapsto x\}\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}}[x\mapsto a])}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket u\{0\mapsto x\}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime},\xi_{\mathsf{te}}^{\prime}[x\mapsto a])}}\quad\text{(by induction hypothesis)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket\lambda\langle\tau\rangle\>u\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}(a)\quad\text{(since $\mathscr{I}$ is proper)}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}(a)

Lemma 23

(Substitution Lemma for Clauses)
.

Let
\theta
be a substitution, and let
C
be a clause.
For any proper interpretation
\mathscr{I}=(\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}},\mathscr{J},\mathscr{L})
and any valuation
\xi
,

C\theta
is true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi
if and only if

C
is true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi^{\prime}
,
where the modified valuation
\xi^{\prime}
is defined
by
\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime}(\alpha)=\smash{\llbracket\alpha\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}}}

for type variables
\alpha

and
\xi_{\mathsf{te}}^{\prime}(x)=\smash{\llbracket x\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}
for term variables
x
.

Proof 8.2
.

By definition of the semantics of clauses,

C\theta
is true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi
if and only if
one of its literals is true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi
.
By definition of the semantics of literals,
a positive literal
s\theta\approx t\theta
(resp. negative literal
s\theta\not\approx t\theta
)
of
C\theta
is
true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi
if and only if

\smash{\llbracket s\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}
and
\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}
are equal (resp. different).
By Lemma
22
,

\smash{\llbracket s\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}
and
\smash{\llbracket t\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}}
are equal (resp. different)
if and only if
\smash{\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}
and
\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}
are equal (resp. different)—i.e.,
if and only if a literal
s\approx t
(resp.
s\not\approx t
) in
C
is true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi^{\prime}
.
This holds if and only if
C
is true
w.r.t.

\mathscr{I}
and
\xi^{\prime}
.

Theorem 24
.

All core inference rules are sound
w.r.t.

\mathrel{|\kern-0.43057pt}\joinrel\approx
(Definition
3.1
).
All core inference rules except for
Ext
,
FluidExt
, and
Diff
are also sound
w.r.t.

\models
.
This holds even when ignoring order, selection, and eligibility conditions.

Proof 8.3
.

We fix an inference and an interpretation
\mathscr{I}
that is a model of the premises.
For
Ext
,
FluidExt
, and
Diff
inferences, we assume that
\mathscr{I}
is
{\mathsf{diff}}
-aware.
We need to show that it is also a model of the conclusion.
By Lemma
23
,
\mathscr{I}
is a model of the
\sigma
-instances of the premises as well, where

\sigma
is the substitution used for the inference.
From the semantics of our logic, it is easy to see that congruence
holds at green positions and at the left subterm of an application.
To show that
\mathscr{I}
is a model of the conclusion, it suffices to show that the conclusion
is true under
\mathscr{I},\xi
for all valuations
\xi
.

For most rules, it suffices to make
distinctions on the truth under
\mathscr{I},\xi
of the literals of the
\sigma
-instances of the premises,
to consider the conditions that
\sigma
is a unifier where applicable,
and to apply congruence.
For
BoolHoist
,
LoobHoist
,
FalseElim
,
Clausify
,
FluidBoolHoist
,
FluidLoobHoist
,
we also use the fact that
\mathscr{I}
interprets logical symbols correctly.
For
Ext
,
FluidExt
, and
Diff
,
we also use the assumption that
\mathscr{I}
is
{\mathsf{diff}}
-aware.

9.
Refutational Completeness

Superposition is a saturation-based calculus.
Provers that implement it start from an initial clause set
N_{0}

and
repeatedly add new clauses by performing inferences
or remove clauses by determining them to be redundant.
In the limit, this process results in a (possibly infinite)
set
N_{\infty}
of persistent clauses.
Assume that inferences are performed in a fair fashion; i.e., no nonredundant
inference is postponed forever.
Then the set
N_{\infty}
is saturated, meaning that all
inferences are redundant (for example because their conclusion is in the set).
Refutational completeness is the property that
if
N_{\infty}
does not contain the empty clause,
N_{0}
has a model.
Since refutational completeness is the only kind of completeness that interests
us in this article, we will also refer to it as “completeness.”

Due the role of constraints and parameters in our calculus,
our completeness result, stated in Corollary
90
, makes two additional assumptions:
It assumes that
the clauses in
N_{0}

have no constraints and do not contain constants with parameters.
And, instead of the usual assumption that
N_{\infty}
does not contain the empty clause,
we assume that
N_{\infty}
does not contain an empty clause with satisfiable constraints.

9.1.
Proof Outline

The idea of superposition completeness proofs in general is the following:
We assume that
N_{\infty}
does not contain the empty clause.
We construct a term rewrite system derived from the ground instances
of
N_{\infty}
.
We view this system as an interpretation
\mathscr{I}
and show that it is
a model of the ground instances and thus of
N_{\infty}
itself.
Since only redundant clauses are removed during saturation,

\mathscr{I}
must also be a model of
N_{0}
.

Completeness proofs of
constrained
superposition calculi,
including our the completeness proof of our calculus,
must proceed differently.
The constraints prevent us from showing
\mathscr{I}
to be a model
of all ground instances of
N_{\infty}
.
Instead, we restrict ourselves to proving that
\mathscr{I}
is a model
of the variable-irreducible ground instances of
N_{\infty}
.
Roughly speaking, a variable-irreducible ground instance is one where
the terms used to instantiate variables
are irreducible
w.r.t.
the constructed term rewrite system.
The notion of redundancy must be based on
the notion of variable-irreducible ground instances as well,
so that if
\mathscr{I}
is
a model
of the variable-irreducible ground instances of
N_{\infty}
,
it is also a model of the
variable-irreducible ground instances of
N_{0}
.
Assuming that the initial clauses
N_{0}
do
not have constraints,
\mathscr{I}

is then a model of all ground instances of
N_{0}

because every ground instance has a corresponding
variable-irreducible instance with the same truth value in
\mathscr{I}
.
It follows that

\mathscr{I}
is a model of
N_{0}
.

higher-order
constrained clauses
\mathrm{G}
higher-order closures
\mathrm{PG}
partly substituted
higher-order closures
\mathrm{IPG}
indexed partly substituted
higher-order closures
\mathrm{PF}
partly substituted

{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>({\mathsf{diff}}^{\iota,\iota}_{({\mathsf{g}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt},{\mathsf{h}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt})})\>(\lambda{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>{\mathsf{k}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>0\>z_{1.2})\approx{\mathsf{c}}
\cdot\ \{y_{1}\mapsto{\mathsf{a}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.83328pt},\ z_{1.2}\mapsto{\mathsf{a}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\}
{\mathsf{f}}^{\iota}\>({\mathsf{diff}}^{\iota,\iota}_{({\mathsf{g}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt},{\mathsf{h}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt})},\>{\mathsf{fun}}_{\lambda{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt}\>{\mathsf{k}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt}\>0\>\square}(z_{1.2}))\approx{\mathsf{c}}
\cdot\ \{y_{1}\mapsto{\mathsf{a}}^{\iota}_{0},\ z_{1.2}\mapsto{\mathsf{a}}^{\iota}_{0}\}
{\mathsf{f}}^{\iota}_{1}\>({\mathsf{diff}}^{\iota,\iota}_{({\mathsf{g}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt},{\mathsf{h}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt}),0},\>{\mathsf{fun}}_{\lambda{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt}\>{\mathsf{k}}{\langle\iota\rangle\kern-0.68283pt}\>0\>\square}({\mathsf{a}}^{\iota}_{0}))\approx{\mathsf{c}}
\mathcalx{G}
\mathcalx{P}
\mathcalx{J}
\mathcalx{F}
\mathcalx{T}

Figure 1.
Overview of the levels

To separate concerns, our proof is structured as a sequence of six
levels, most of which have their own
logic, calculus, redundancy criterion, and completeness property.
The levels are called

\mathrm{H}
,
\mathrm{G}
,
\mathrm{PG}
,
\mathrm{IPG}
,
\mathrm{PF}
, and
\mathrm{F}
.
They are connected by functions encoding clauses from one level to the next.

The level
\mathrm{H}
is the level of higher-order constrained clauses,
using the logic described
in Section
2
and the calculus described in Section
4
.
Our ultimate goal is to prove completeness on this level.

The level
\mathrm{G}
is the level of higher-order closures,
where a closure
C\cdot\theta
is a pair consisting of a clause
C
and
a grounding substitution
\theta
.
The function
\mathcalx{G}

maps each clause from level
\mathrm{H}
to a corresponding set of closures on
level
\mathrm{G}

using all possible grounding substitutions.

The level
\mathrm{PG}
is the level of
partly substituted

higher-order closures. It is the fragment of
\mathrm{G}

that contains no type variables and no functional variables.
The map
\mathcalx{P}
encodes closures from
\mathrm{G}

into level
\mathrm{PG}
by applying a carefully crafted
substitution to functional variables.

The level
\mathrm{IPG}
is the level of
indexed

partly substituted closures. It modifies the signature of the previous levels
by replacing each symbol with parameters

{\mathsf{f}}:\mathsf{\Pi}\bar{\alpha}_{m}.\;\>\bar{\tau}_{n}\Rightarrow\tau

by a collection of symbols

{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}}_{\bar{u}_{n}}:\tau

for each tuple of
types
\bar{\upsilon}_{m}
and
each tuple of ground terms
\bar{u}_{n}:\bar{\tau}_{n}
.
The map
\mathcalx{J}
encodes closures from
\mathrm{PG}

into
\mathrm{IPG}
by moving
type arguments into the superscript indices
\bar{\upsilon}_{m}

parameters into the subscript
indices
\bar{u}_{n}
.

The level
\mathrm{PF}
is the level of partly substituted
ground first-order closures.
Its logic is the one described in Section
6.2

except with variables and closures.
We extend the encoding
\mathcalx{F}
(Definition
6.2
)
with variables, yielding an encoding from
\mathrm{IPG}

into
\mathrm{PF}
.

The level
\mathrm{F}
is the level of first-order clauses.
It uses the same logic as
\mathrm{PF}
but uses ground clauses
instead of closures. The map
\mathcalx{T}
connects the two by
mapping a closure
C\cdot\theta
to the clause
C\theta
.

Figure
1
gives
an overview of the hierarchy of levels
and an example of a clause instance across the levels.

9.2.
Logics and Encodings

In our completeness proof, we use two higher-order signatures and one first-order signature.

Let
\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}}
be the higher-order signature
used by the calculus described in Section
4
.
It is required to contain a symbol

{\mathsf{diff}}:\Pi\alpha,\beta.\>(\alpha\rightarrow\beta,\alpha\rightarrow\beta)\Rightarrow\alpha

Let
\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}}
be the signature obtained from

\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}}
in the following way:
We replace each constant with parameters

{{\mathsf{f}}:\mathsf{\Pi}\bar{\alpha}_{m}.\;\bar{\tau}_{n}\Rightarrow\tau}
in
\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}}

with a family of constants

{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}}_{\bar{t}_{n}}:\tau
, indexed by all possible ground types

\bar{\upsilon}_{m}
and ground terms

\bar{t}_{n}\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
of type
\bar{\tau}_{n}\{\bar{\alpha}_{m}\mapsto\bar{\upsilon}_{m}\}
.
Constants without parameters (even those with type arguments) are left as they are.

In some contexts,
it is more convenient to
use terms from
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
instead of
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})

in the subscripts
t_{i}
of the constants
{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}}_{\bar{t}_{n}}
.
We follow this convention:

{conv}

In the subscripts
t_{i}
of constants
{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}}_{\bar{t}_{n}}\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}}
,
we identify each term of the form

{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}_{m}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(\bar{t}_{n})\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})

with the term

{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}}_{\bar{t}_{n}}\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
,
whenever
n>0
.

Similarly, the first-order signatures
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
and
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})

as defined in Section
6.2

are almost identical, the only difference being that
the subscripts
t
of the symbols
{\mathsf{fun}}_{t}\in\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})

may contain symbols with parameters,
whereas the subscripts
t
of the symbols
{\mathsf{fun}}_{t}\in\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})

may not. To repair this mismatch, we adopt the following convention
using the obvious correspondence between the symbols in
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
and
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
:

{conv}

In the subscripts of constants
{\mathsf{fun}}_{t}
in
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
and
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
,
we identify each term of the form

{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}_{m}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(\bar{t}_{n})\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})

with the term

{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}}_{\bar{t}_{n}}\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
,
whenever
n>0
.
Using this identification,
we can consider the first-order signatures
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
and
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})

to be identical.

Our completeness proof uses two sets of variables.
Let
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
be the set of variables
used by the calculus described in Section
4
.
Based on
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
, we define the variables
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}
of the

\mathrm{PG}
level as

\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}=\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}\cup\{y_{p}\langle\tau\rangle\mid y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}},\ p\text{ a list of natural numbers},\ \tau\text{ a nonfunctional type}\}

The table below summarizes our completeness proof’s six levels, each with a set
of terms and a set of clauses. We write
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{X}}
for the set of terms
and
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{X}}
for the set of clauses of a given level
X
:

Level

Terms

Clauses

\mathrm{F}

ground first-order terms over
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})

clauses over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{F}}

\mathrm{PF}

first-order terms over
\mathcalx{F}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
and
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}

that do not contain variables whose type is of the form

\tau\rightarrow\upsilon

closures over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}

\mathrm{IPG}

\{t\in\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}},\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}})\mid

t
contains neither type variables nor functional variables
\}

closures over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

\mathrm{PG}

\{t\in\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}},\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}})\mid

t
contains neither type variables nor functional variables
\}

closures over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PG}}

\mathrm{G}

\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}},\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}})

closures over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{G}}

\mathrm{H}

\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}},\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}})

constrained clauses over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{H}}

9.2.1.
First-Order Encodings

The transformation
\mathcalx{T}
from
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
to
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{F}}
is simply defined as
\mathcalx{T}(C\cdot\theta)=C\theta
.
We also define a bijective encoding from

\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
into

\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}

and from

\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
into

\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
.
It is very similar to the encoding
\mathcalx{F}:\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})\to\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{F}}

defined in Definition
6.2
,
but also encodes variables and does not encode parameters.
We reuse the name
\mathcalx{F}
for this new encoding.
Potential for confusion is minimal because the two encodings coincide on the values that are in the domain of both.

{defi}

[First-Order Encoding
\mathcalx{F}
]
We define
\mathcalx{F}:\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}\to\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
recursively as follows:
If
t
is functional,
then
let
t^{\prime}
be the expression
obtained by replacing each
outermost proper yellow subterm in
t

by the placeholder symbol
\square
,
and let
\mathcalx{F}(t)={\mathsf{fun}}_{t^{\prime}}(\mathcalx{F}(\bar{s}_{n}))
, where
\bar{s}_{n}

are the replaced subterms in order of occurrence.
If
t
is a variable
x
, we define
\mathcalx{F}(t)=x
.
Otherwise,
t
is of the form
{\mathsf{f}}\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\>\bar{t}_{m}

and we define
\mathcalx{F}(t)={\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\tau}}(\mathcalx{F}(\bar{t}_{1}),\dots,\mathcalx{F}(\bar{t}_{m}))
.

Applied to a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
, the function
\mathcalx{F}

is defined by
\mathcalx{F}\!(C\cdot\theta)=\mathcalx{F}\!(C)\cdot\mathcalx{F}\!(\theta)
,
where
\mathcalx{F}
maps each side of each literal
and each term in a substitution individually.

Lemma 25
.

The map
\mathcalx{F}
is a bijection between
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
and
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}

and between
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
and
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
.

Proof 9.1
.

Injectivity of
\mathcalx{F}
can be shown by structural induction.
For surjectivity, let
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
.
We must show that there exists some
s\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
such that
\mathcalx{F}(s)=t
.
We proceed by induction on
t
.

If
t
is of the form
{\mathsf{fun}}_{t^{\prime}}(\bar{t}_{n})
,
we use the induction hypothesis to derive the existence of
some
\bar{s}_{n}\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

such that
\mathcalx{F}(\bar{s}_{n})=\bar{t}_{n}
.
Let
s
be the term resulting from replacing the placeholder symbols
\square
in
t^{\prime}
by
\bar{s}_{n}
in order of occurrence.
Then
\mathcalx{F}(s)=t
.

If
t
is a variable
x
, by definition of
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
,
t
’s type is not of the form
\tau\rightarrow\upsilon
.
So, we can set
s=x\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
. Then
\mathcalx{F}(s)=t
.

If
t={\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\tau}}(\bar{t}_{n})
, where
{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\tau}}
is not a
{\mathsf{fun}}
symbol,
by the induction hypothesis
there exist
\bar{s}_{n}
such that
\mathcalx{F}(\bar{s}_{n})=\bar{t}_{n}
and set
s={\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>\bar{s}_{n}
. Then
\mathcalx{F}(s)=t
.

It follows that
\mathcalx{F}
is also a bijection between
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
and
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
.

Lemma 26
.

For all terms
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
,
all clauses over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
,
and all grounding substitutions
\theta
, we have

\mathcalx{F}(t)\mathcalx{F}(\theta)=\mathcalx{F}(t\theta)

and

\mathcalx{F}(C)\mathcalx{F}(\theta)=\mathcalx{F}(C\theta)
.

Proof 9.2
.

Since
\mathcalx{F}
maps each side of each literal individually,
it suffices to show that
\mathcalx{F}(t)\mathcalx{F}(\theta)=\mathcalx{F}(t\theta)

for all
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
.
We proceed by structural induction on
t
.

If
t
is a variable, the claim is trivial.

If
t
is nonfunctional and headed by a symbol, the claim follows from the induction hypothesis.

Finally, we consider the case where
t
is functional.
Let
t^{\prime}
be the expression
obtained by replacing each
outermost proper yellow subterm in
t

by the placeholder symbol
\square
,
and let
\bar{s}_{n}

be the replaced subterms in order of occurrence.
Since all variables in
t
are nonfunctional,
they must be located in a proper yellow subterm of
t
,
and thus replacing
the outermost proper yellow subterm in
t\theta

by the placeholder symbol
\square

will result in
t^{\prime}
as well.
So, using the induction hypothesis,

\mathcalx{F}(t)\mathcalx{F}(\theta)={\mathsf{fun}}_{t^{\prime}}(\mathcalx{F}(\bar{s}_{n})\mathcalx{F}(\theta))={\mathsf{fun}}_{t^{\prime}}(\mathcalx{F}(\bar{s}_{n}\theta))=\mathcalx{F}(t\theta)
.

Lemma 27
.

A term
s\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
is a yellow subterm of
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
if and only if
\mathcalx{F}(s)

is a subterm of
\mathcalx{F}(t)
.

Proof 9.3
.

By induction using the definition of
\mathcalx{F}
.

Lemma 28
.

A term
s\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
is a green subterm of
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
if and only if
\mathcalx{F}(s)

is a green subterm (as defined in Section
6.2
) of
\mathcalx{F}(t)
.

Proof 9.4
.

By induction using the definition of
\mathcalx{F}
.

9.2.2.
Indexing of Parameters

{defi}

[Indexing of Parameters]
The transformation
\mathcalx{J}
translates from
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PG}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
by
encoding any occurrence of a constant with parameters
{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(\bar{u})
as

{\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}}_{\bar{u}\theta}
,
where
\theta
denotes the substitution of the corresponding closure.
Formally:

\displaystyle\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(x)

\displaystyle=x

\displaystyle\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(\lambda\>t)

\displaystyle=\lambda\>\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(t)

\displaystyle\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}({\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>\bar{s})

\displaystyle={\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(\bar{s})

\displaystyle\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}({\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>(\bar{u}_{k})\>\bar{s})

\displaystyle={\mathsf{f}}^{\bar{\upsilon}}_{\bar{u}_{k}\theta}\>\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(\bar{s})\text{ if $k>0$}

\displaystyle\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(m\>\bar{s})

\displaystyle=m\>\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(\bar{s})

We extend
\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}
to clauses by mapping each side of each literal individually.

If
t
is a ground term, the given substitution is irrelevant, so we omit the subscript and simply write
\mathcalx{J}(t)
.
We extend
\mathcalx{J}
to grounding substitutions by
defining
\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
as
x\mapsto\mathcalx{J}(x\theta)
.
The transformation
\mathcalx{J}
w.r.t. a closure
C\cdot\theta
is defined as
\mathcalx{J}(C\cdot\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(C)\cdot\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
.

Lemma 29
.

For all
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PG}}
,
all clauses
C
over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PG}}
,
and all grounding substitutions
\theta
, we have

\mathcalx{J}(t\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(t)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)

and
\mathcalx{J}(C\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(C)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
.

Proof 9.5
.

Since
\mathcalx{J}
maps each side of each literal individually,
it suffices to show that

\mathcalx{J}(t\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(t)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
.
We prove this by induction on the structure of
t
.
If
t
is a variable, the claim is trivial.
For all other cases, the claim follows from the definition of
\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}

and the induction hypothesis.

Lemma 30
.

If

\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(t)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(t^{\prime})\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
,
then

t\theta=t^{\prime}\theta
.

Proof 9.6
.

This becomes clear when viewing
\mathcalx{J}

as composed of two operations: First,
we apply the substitution to all variables in
parameters. Second, we move type arguments and
parameters into indices.
Both parts clearly fulfill this lemma’s statement.

Lemma 31
.

Let
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
, and
let
C
be a clause over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
.
Then
\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(t))=\mathcalx{F}(t)

and
\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(C))=\mathcalx{F}(C)
.

Proof 9.7
.

For
t
, the claim follows directly from
the definitions of
\mathcalx{J}
(Definition
9.2.2
) and
\mathcalx{F}

(Definitions
6.2
and
9.2.1
),
relying on the identification of
{\mathsf{fun}}_{t}
and
{\mathsf{fun}}_{\mathcalx{J}(t)}
(Convention
9.2
).
For
C
, the claim holds because

\mathcalx{J}
and
\mathcalx{F}
map each side of each literal individually.

9.2.3.
Partial Substitution

Let
\theta
be a grounding substitution from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
. We define a substitution

\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
, mapping from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
to
\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}},\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}})
, and
a substitution
\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
,
mapping from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
,
as follows.
For each type variable
\alpha
,
let
\alpha\mathfrak{p}(\theta)=\alpha\theta
.
For each variable
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
, let
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
be the term resulting
from replacing each nonfunctional yellow subterm at a yellow position
p
in
y\theta
by

y_{p}\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}
.
We call these variables
y_{p}
the variables introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.
If a nonfunctional yellow subterm is contained inside another nonfunctional yellow subterm,
the outermost nonfunctional yellow subterm is replaced by a variable.
The substitution

\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
is defined
as
y_{p}\mathfrak{q}(\theta)=y\theta|_{p}

for all variables
y_{p}
introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
,
and for all other variables
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}
, we set

y\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
to be some arbitrary ground term that is independent of
\theta
.

Finally, we define

\mathcalx{P}:\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{G}}\to\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}},\quad C\cdot\theta\mapsto C\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\cdot\mathfrak{q}(\theta)

For example, if
y\theta=\lambda\>{\mathsf{f}}\>(0\>({\mathsf{g}}\>{\mathsf{a}}))
,
then
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)=\lambda\>{\mathsf{f}}\>(0\>y_{1.1.1})

and
y_{1.1.1}\mathfrak{q}(\theta)={\mathsf{g}}\>{\mathsf{a}}
.

Technically, this definition of
\mathfrak{p}
,
\mathfrak{q}
, and
\mathcalx{P}

depends on the choice of a
\beta\eta
-normalizer
\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta\eta}

because it relies on yellow positions. However,
this choice affects the resulting terms and clauses only up to
renaming of variables, and our proofs
work for any choice of
\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta\eta}

as long as we use the
same fixed
\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta\eta}

for
\mathfrak{p}
,
\mathfrak{q}
, and
\mathcalx{P}
.

Lemma 32
.

Let
\theta
be a grounding substitution. Then

\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\mathfrak{q}(\theta)=\theta
.

Proof 9.8
.

For type variables
\alpha
, we have
\alpha\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\mathfrak{q}(\theta)=\alpha\theta
by definition of
\mathfrak{p}
.
We must show that
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\mathfrak{q}(\theta)=y\theta
for all variables
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
By definition of
\mathfrak{p}
,
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
is obtained from
y\theta
by replacing each nonfunctional yellow subterm at a yellow position
p
with
y_{p}
.
By definition of
\mathfrak{q}
, we have
y_{p}\mathfrak{q}(\theta)=y\theta|_{p}
for all such positions
p
.
Therefore, when we apply
\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
to
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
, we replace each
y_{p}
with the original subterm
y\theta|_{p}
, effectively reconstructing
y\theta
.

Lemma 33
.

Let
\theta
be a substitution from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
and
\rho
be a substitution
from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
.
Then

\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.

Proof 9.9
.

Let
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
By definition of
\mathfrak{p}
,
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
is obtained from
y\theta

by replacing each nonfunctional yellow subterm at a yellow position
p
with
y_{p}
.
Now, consider
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho
. Since
\rho
is grounding,
it will replace each
y_{p}
with a ground term.
To obtain
y\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)
, we take
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho
and again replace each nonfunctional yellow subterm at a yellow position
p
with
y_{p}
.
These positions and the resulting structure will be identical to those in
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)

because the ground terms introduced by
\rho
do not affect the overall structure of yellow positions.
Therefore,
y\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
for each variable
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
.

For type variables
\alpha
, we have
\alpha\mathfrak{p}(\theta)=\alpha\theta=\alpha\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)
.
Thus, we can conclude that
\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.

Lemma 34
.

Let
\theta
be a substitution from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
.
Let
\rho
be a substitution
from
\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{PG}}
to
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})

such that
y\rho=y\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
for all
y
not introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.
Then

\mathfrak{q}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=\rho
.

Proof 9.10
.

Let
y_{p}
be a variable introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)
.
By definition of
\mathfrak{q}
, we have
y_{p}\mathfrak{q}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho|_{p}
.
Moreover, since
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)|_{p}=y_{p}
, we have
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho|_{p}=y_{p}\rho
.
So
y_{p}\mathfrak{q}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=y_{p}\rho
.

Let
y
be a variable not introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)
.
It remains to show that
y\mathfrak{q}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=y\rho
.
By Lemma
33
,
the variables introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)

are the same as the variables introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)
.
So
y
is not introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
either.
So, by definition of
\mathfrak{q}
, we have
y\mathfrak{q}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=y\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
, and
with the assumption of this lemma that
y\rho=y\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
,
we conclude that
y\mathfrak{q}(\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\rho)=y\rho
.

Lemma 35
.

Let
\theta
be a grounding substitution.
For each variable
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
,

y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
is the most general term
t
(unique up to renaming of variables) with the following properties:

1.

there exists a substitution
\rho
such that
t\rho=y\theta
;

2.

t
contains no type variables and no functional variables.

Proof 9.11
.

Let
y\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
By Lemma
32
,
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
satisfies property
1
,
and by definition of
\mathfrak{p}
, it satisfies property
2
.

To show that
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
is the most general such term,
let
s
be any term satisfying properties
1
and
2
,
and let
\sigma
be a substitution such that
s\sigma=y\theta
.
We must show there exists a substitution
\pi
such that
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\pi=s
.

Since
s
contains no type variables and no functional variables,
it is easy to see from the definition of orange subterms
that for any orange position
p
of
s\sigma
, either
p

is also an orange position of
s
or there exists a proper prefix
q
of
p
such that
q
is an orange position of
s

and
s|_{q}
is a nonfunctional variable.
If there exists such a prefix
q
, then
q
must be a nonfunctional yellow position of
s\sigma

since
\sigma
cannot introduce free De Bruijn indices at that position,
and thus
p
cannot be an outermost nonfunctional yellow subterm of
s\sigma
.
From these observations, we conclude that any outermost nonfunctional yellow position
p
of
s\sigma

must be an orange position of
s
.
In fact, since substituting
nonfunctional variables
cannot eliminate De Bruijn indices,
any outermost nonfunctional yellow position of
s\sigma

must be a yellow position of
s
.

Let
\pi
map each variable
y_{p}
introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)

to the corresponding term in
s
at position
p
.
This term exists because
p
is, by definition of
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
,
an outermost nonfunctional yellow position of
y\theta=s\sigma

and thus, by the above, a yellow position of
s
.
Then
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\pi=s
by construction,
showing that
y\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
is indeed most general.

Lemma 36
.

Let
\sigma
be a substitution, and let
\zeta
be a grounding substitution.
Then there exists a substitution
\pi
such that

\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)=\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)\pi

and

\mathfrak{q}(\sigma\zeta)=\pi\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)
.

Proof 9.12
.

Let
x\in\mathscr{V}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
By Lemma
32
,

x\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)=x\sigma\zeta
.
Moreover,
x\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)
contains only nonfunctional variables.
By Lemma
35
, since
x\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)
is the most general term
with these properties, there must exist a substitution
\pi
such that

x\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)=x\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)\pi
.
Since the variables in
x_{1}\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)
and
x_{2}\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)

are disjoint for
x_{1}\neq x_{2}
,
we can construct a single substitution
\pi
that satisfies
\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)=\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)\pi
,
proving the first part of the lemma.

For this construction of
\pi
, only the values of
\pi
for
variables introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)
are relevant.
Thus, we can define
y\pi=y\mathfrak{q}(\sigma\zeta)
for all other variables
y
.
Then
y\mathfrak{q}(\sigma\zeta)=y\pi\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)
for all variables
y
not introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)
.

Finally, let
y_{p}
be a variable introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)
.
By Lemma
32
and the above,

\sigma\zeta=\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)=\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)\pi\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)
.
By Lemma
34
,

y_{p}\mathfrak{q}(\sigma\zeta)=y_{p}\pi\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)

for all variables
y_{p}
introduced by
\mathfrak{p}(\sigma\zeta)
,
completing the proof of the second part of the lemma.

The redundancy notions of the
\mathrm{H}
level use the map
\mathcalx{F}
,
defined in Section
6.2
.
It is closely related to the maps defined above.

Lemma 37
.

For all clauses
C
and grounding substitutions
\theta
,

\mathcalx{F}(C\theta)=\mathcalx{T}(\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(\mathcalx{P}(C\cdot\theta))))

Proof 9.13
.

All of the maps
\mathcalx{T}
,
\mathcalx{F}
,
\mathcalx{J}
, and
\mathcalx{P}

map each literal and each side of a literal individually.
So we can focus on one side
s
of some literal in
C
,
and we must show that

\mathcalx{F}(s\theta)=\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}_{\mathfrak{q}(\theta)}(s\mathfrak{p}(\theta)))\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(\mathfrak{q}(\theta)))

By Lemma
31
,

\mathcalx{F}(t)=\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(t))

for all ground terms
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
.
By Lemma
29
,

\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(t)\mathcalx{J}(\rho)=\mathcalx{J}(t\rho)

for all
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PG}}
and grounding substitutions
\rho
.
Also, by Lemma
26
,

\mathcalx{F}(t)\mathcalx{F}(\rho)=\mathcalx{F}(t\rho)

for all
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
and grounding substitutions
\rho
.
From the last three equations, we obtain that

\mathcalx{F}(t\rho)=\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(t))\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(\rho))

for all
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PG}}
and grounding substitutions
\rho
.

Using the term
s
and the substitution
\theta
introduced at the beginning of this proof,
take
t
to be
s\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
and
\rho
to be
\mathfrak{q}(\theta)
.
We then have

\mathcalx{F}(s\mathfrak{p}(\theta)\mathfrak{q}(\theta))=\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}_{\mathfrak{q}(\theta)}(s\mathfrak{p}(\theta)))\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(\mathfrak{q}(\theta)))

By Lemma
32
, this implies (
*
).

9.2.4.
Grounding

The terms of level
\mathrm{H}
are
\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
.
Its clauses
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
are constrained clauses over these terms.
We define the function
\mathcalx{G}:\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}\to\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{G}}
by

\mathcalx{G}(C[\![S]\!])=\{C\cdot\theta\mid\theta\text{ is grounding and }S\theta\text{ is true}\}

for each constrained clause
C[\![S]\!]\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
.

9.3.
Calculi

In this section, we define the calculi

\mathit{PFInf}
,
\mathit{IPGInf}
, and
\mathit{PGInf}
,
for the respective levels

\mathrm{PF}
,
\mathrm{IPG}
, and
\mathrm{PG}
. Each of these calculi is
parameterized by
a relation
\succ
on
ground terms, ground clauses, and closures
and by a selection function
\mathit{sel}
.

Based on these parameters, we define
the notion of eligibility.

The specific requirements on
\succ
depend on the calculus and are given
in the corresponding subsection below.

For each of the levels, we define selection functions and
the notion of eligibility as follows:

{defi}
[Selection Function]
For each level
X\in\{\mathrm{PF},\mathrm{IPG},\mathrm{PG}\}
,
we define
a selection function
\mathit{sel}
to be a function mapping each closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{X}
to
a subset of
C
’s literals. We call those literals
selected
.
Only negative literals and
literals of the form
t\approx\kern 0.17224pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\bot$}\kern 0.17224pt
may be selected.

{defi}

[Eligibility in Closures]
Let
X\in\{\mathrm{PF},\mathrm{IPG},\mathrm{PG}\}
.
Let
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{X}
.
Given a relation
\succ

and a selection function,
a literal
L\in C
is (
strictly
)
eligible
in
C\cdot\theta
if it is
selected in
C\cdot\theta

or there are no selected literals in
C\cdot\theta

and
L\theta
is (strictly) maximal in
C\theta
.
A position

L.s.p

of a closure
C\cdot\theta
is
eligible

if the literal
L
is
of the form
s\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}t
with
s\theta\succ t\theta

and
L
is either
negative and
eligible
or positive and strictly eligible.

For inferences, we follow the same conventions as in Definition
6.1
,
but our inference rules operate on closures instead of constrained clauses.

10.0.1.
Indexed Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

The
calculus
\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ,\mathit{sel}}
is parameterized
by a relation
\succ
and a selection function
\mathit{sel}
.
We require that
\succ
is an admissible term order for
\mathit{IPGInf}
in the following sense:

{defi}

Let
\succ
be a relation
on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})

on clauses over

\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

11.0.1.
Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

Like on the other levels,
the calculus
\mathit{PGInf}
is parameterized
by a relation
\succ
and a selection function
\mathit{sel}
.

{defi}

Let
\succ
be a relation on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
, on clauses over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
, and on
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
.
Such a relation
\succ
is
an admissible term order for
\mathit{PGInf}

if it fulfills the following properties:

(\text{O1})_{\mathrm{PG}}

the relation
\succ
on ground terms is a well-founded total order;

(\text{O2})_{\mathrm{PG}}

ground compatibility with yellow contexts:
s^{\prime}\succ s
implies

, and

12.1.
Redundancy Criteria and Saturation

In this subsection, we define redundancy criteria
for the levels

\mathrm{PF}
,
\mathrm{IPG}
,
\mathrm{PG}
, and
\mathrm{H}

and show that saturation up to redundancy on one level implies saturation up to
redundancy on the previous level.
We will use these results in Section
12.3
to lift
refutational completeness from level
\mathrm{PF}
to level
\mathrm{H}
.

{defi}

A set
N
of clauses is called
saturated up to redundancy

if every inference with premises in
N
is redundant
w.r.t.

N
.

12.1.1.
First-Order Level

In this subsection, let
\succ
be an admissible term order for

(Definition

),
and let

We define a notion of variable-irreducibility,
roughly following Nieuwenhuis and Rubio

and Bachmair et al.

{defi}

Given a set

for the set of variable-irreducible closures in

Remark 38
.

The restriction that
L\theta\succ s\approx t

cannot be replaced by
C\theta\succ s\approx t

because we need it to ensure that
\mathrm{irred}_{R}(N)
is saturated when
N
is.

Here is an example demonstrating that variable-irreducibilty would not
be closed under inferences if we used the entire clause for comparison:
Let
{\mathsf{e}}\succ{\mathsf{d}}\succ{\mathsf{c}}\succ{\mathsf{b}}\succ{\mathsf{a}}
and

R=\{{\mathsf{e}}\rightarrow{\mathsf{b}}\}
. Then a notion replacing the restriction
L\theta\succ s\approx t

by
C\theta\succ s\approx t

would say that

x\approx{\mathsf{a}}\mathrel{\lor}x\approx{\mathsf{b}}\ [\![x\equiv{\mathsf{e}}]\!]

and

{\mathsf{e}}\approx{\mathsf{c}}\mathrel{\lor}{\mathsf{e}}\approx{\mathsf{d}}

are order-irreducible
w.r.t.

R
. By
Sup
(second literal of the first clause into
the second literal of the second clause), we obtain

x\approx{\mathsf{a}}\mathrel{\lor}{\mathsf{e}}\approx{\mathsf{c}}\mathrel{\lor}{\mathsf{b}}\approx{\mathsf{d}}\ [\![x\equiv e]\!]

Now
x\theta
in the first literal has become order-reducible by
{\mathsf{e}}\rightarrow{\mathsf{b}}

since
e\approx b
is now smaller than the largest literal
e\approx c
of the clause.

To connect to the redundancy criteria of the higher levels, we need to establish

Lemma 39
.

Let

12.1.2.
Indexed Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

In this subsubsection, let
\succ
be an admissible term order for
\mathit{IPGInf}
(Definition
10.0.1
),
and let
\mathit{ipgsel}
be a selection function on

\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
(Definition
9.3
).

To lift the notion of inference redundancy, we need to connect the inference systems

\mathit{PFInf}
and
\mathit{IPGInf}
as follows.

Since the mapping
\mathcalx{F}
is bijective (Lemma
25
),
we can transfer the order
\succ
from the
\mathrm{IPG}
level to the
\mathrm{PF}
level:

{defi}

Based on
\succ
,
we define
a relation
\succ{F}

on ground terms
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{F}}
, ground clauses

\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{F}}
, and closures
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
as

d\mathrel{\succ{F}}e
if and only if
\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(d)\succ\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(e)

for all terms, clauses, or closures
d
and
e
.

Lemma 40
.

Since
\succ
is an admissible term order for
\mathit{IPGInf}
(Definition
10.0.1
),
the relation
\succ{F}
is an admissible term order for
\mathit{PFInf}
(Definition
9.3.1
).

Proof 12.2
.

This is easy to see, considering
that
\mathcalx{F}
is a bijection between
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
and
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}^{\mathsf{gnd}}

(Lemma
25
),
that higher-order yellow subterms and first-order subterms correspond
by Lemma
27
,
that

\mathcalx{F}
maps each side of each literal individually,
and that
\mathcalx{F}(C)\mathcalx{F}(\theta)=\mathcalx{F}(C\theta)

for all
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
(Lemma
26
).

Since
\mathcalx{F}
is bijective, we can transfer the selection function as follows:

{defi}

Based on
\mathit{ipgsel}
,
we define
\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{ipgsel})
as a selection function that selects
the literals of
C\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
corresponding to the
\mathit{ipgsel}
-selected literals in

\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(C)
.

{defi}

We extend
\mathcalx{F}
to inference rules
by mapping an inference
\iota\in\mathit{IPGInf}

to the inference

\displaystyle{\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{prems}(\iota))}\mathstrut

\displaystyle\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{concl}(\iota))\mathstrut

Lemma 41
.

The mapping
\mathcalx{F}
is a bijection between
\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ,\mathit{ipgsel}}
and

\mathit{PFInf}^{\succ{F},\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{ipgsel})}
.

Proof 12.3
.

This is easy to see by comparing the rules of
\mathit{IPGInf}
and
\mathit{PFInf}
.
It is crucial that the following concepts match:

–

Green subterms on the
\mathrm{PF}
level correspond to green subterms on the
\mathrm{IPG}
level
by Lemma
28
.

–

The term orders correspond (Definition
12.1.2
).

–

The selected literals correspond; i.e.,
a literal
L
is selected in a closure
C\cdot\theta
if and only if
the literal
\mathcalx{F}(L)
is selected in
\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)
.
This follows directly from the definition of
\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{ipgsel})
(Definition
12.1.2
).

–

The concepts of eligibility correspond; i.e.,
a literal
L
of a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

is (strictly) eligible
w.r.t.

\succeq

if and only if
the literal
\mathcalx{F}(L)
of the closure
\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)

is (strictly) eligible
w.r.t.

\succeq{F}
; and
a position
L.s.p
of a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
is eligible
w.r.t.

\succeq

if and only if
the position
\mathcalx{F}(L).\mathcalx{F}(s).q
of the closure
\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)

is eligible
w.r.t.

\succeq{F}
,
where
q
is the position corresponding to
p
.
This is true because eligibility (Definition
9.3
) depends only on the selected literals and the term order,
which correspond as discussed above.

{defi}

Given a term rewrite system
R
on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{F}}
,
we say that a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

\succ{F}
.
We write
\mathrm{irred}_{R}(N)

.

{defi}

[Inference Redundancy]
Given
\iota\in\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ,\mathit{ipgsel}}

Lemma 42
.

Let
\iota_{\mathrm{IPG}}\in\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ,\mathit{ipgsel}}
.
Let
C_{1}\cdot\theta_{1},\dots,C_{m}\cdot\theta_{m}
be its premises
and
C_{m+1}\cdot\theta_{m+1}

Then

\displaystyle{\mathcalx{F}(C_{1}\theta_{1})\cdots\mathcalx{F}(C_{m}\theta_{m})}\mathstrut

\displaystyle\mathcalx{F}(C_{m+1}\theta_{m+1})\mathstrut

\mathit{FInf}^{\succ{F}}

\iota_{\mathrm{F}}
, and

\iota_{\mathrm{IPG}}
and
\iota_{\mathrm{F}}

and

.

Proof 12.4
.

By Lemma
41
, we know that
\mathcalx{F}(\iota_{\mathrm{IPG}})
is a valid
\mathit{PFInf}^{\succ{F},\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{ipgsel})}
inference, and the rule names coincide up to the prefixes
PF
and
IPG
.

Now, applying Lemma
39
to
\mathcalx{F}(\iota_{\mathrm{IPG}})

and using the fact that
\mathcalx{F}(C_{i})\mathcalx{F}(\theta_{i})=\mathcalx{F}(C_{i}\theta_{i})

\displaystyle{\mathcalx{F}(C_{1}\theta_{1})\quad\cdots\quad\mathcalx{F}(C_{m}\theta_{m})}\mathstrut

\iota_{\mathrm{F}}

\mathcalx{F}(\iota_{\mathrm{IPG}})
and

correspond up to the prefixes

and

Combining these two results, we conclude that the rule names of
\iota_{\mathrm{IPG}}
and
\iota_{\mathrm{F}}
correspond up to the prefixes
IPG
and
F
, which completes the proof.

Using the bijection between
\mathit{IPGInf}
and
\mathit{PFInf}
,
we can show that saturation
w.r.t.

\mathit{IPGInf}
implies saturation
w.r.t.

\mathit{PFInf}
:

Lemma 43
.

Let

\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ,\mathit{ipgsel}}
.
Then
\mathcalx{F}(N)
is saturated up to redundancy w.r.t.
\mathit{PFInf}^{\succ{F},\mathcalx{F}(\mathit{ipgsel})}
.

Proof 12.5
.

By Lemma
41

because the notions of inference redundancy correspond.

Since mapping
\mathcalx{J}
is clearly bijective for ground terms and ground clauses,
we can transfer
\succ
from the
\mathrm{PG}
level to the
\mathrm{IPG}

as follows:

{defi}

Let
\succ
be a relation on

\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
, on clauses over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
, and on closures
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
.
We define
a relation
\succ{J}

on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
and
on clauses over
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})

as

d\mathrel{\succ{J}}e
if and only if
\mathcalx{J}^{-1}(d)\succ\mathcalx{J}^{-1}(e)

for all terms or clauses
d
and
e
.
For closures
C\cdot\theta,D\cdot\rho\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
, we
define
C\cdot\theta\mathrel{\succ{J}}D\cdot\rho
if

C\theta\mathrel{\succ{J}}D\rho
.

Lemma 44
.

Since
\succ
is an admissible term order for
\mathit{PGInf}
(Definition
11.0.1
),
the relation
\succ{J}
is an admissible term order for
\mathit{IPGInf}
(Definition
10.0.1
).

Proof 12.6
.

This is easy to see, considering that

\mathcalx{J}
is a bijection on ground terms
and that
\mathcalx{J}
and
\mathcalx{J}^{-1}
preserve yellow subterms.

Lemma 45
.

Given
D\cdot\rho,C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
, we have

D\cdot\rho\succ C\cdot\theta
if and only if

\mathcalx{J}(D\cdot\rho)\mathrel{\succ{J}}\mathcalx{J}(C\cdot\theta)
.

Proof 12.7
.

By

(
O7
)

IPG

,

D\cdot\rho\succ C\cdot\theta
if and only if

C\theta\succ D\rho
.
By Definition
12.1.3
,
this is equivalent to
\mathcalx{J}(D\rho)\mathrel{\succ{J}}\mathcalx{J}(C\theta)
.
Since
\mathcalx{J}(D\rho)=\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(D)\mathcalx{J}(\rho)

and
\mathcalx{J}(C\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(C)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
by Lemma
29
,
this is equivalent to

\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(D)\mathcalx{J}(\rho)\mathrel{\succ{J}}\mathcalx{J}_{\theta}(C)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
.
By

(
O7
)

IPG

, this is equivalent to

\mathcalx{J}(D\cdot\rho)\mathrel{\succ{J}}\mathcalx{J}(C\cdot\theta)
.

{defi}

Given a term rewrite system

on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{F}}

for all variable-irreducible closures in a set

.

{defi}

[Inference Redundancy]

{defi}

Lemma 46
.

Let

\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ{J},\mathcalx{J}(\mathit{pgsel},N)}

Proof 12.8
.

Let
\iota^{\prime}
be a
\mathit{IPGInf}^{\succ{J},\mathcalx{J}(\mathit{pgsel},N)}

from
\mathcalx{J}(N)

We must show that

It suffices to construct a
\mathit{PGInf}

\iota

with premises

coincide up to the prefixes

is satisfied.
Condition

Thus, condition

must be satisfied.
Then, by Definition

,

Finding such an inference

is straightforward for all inference rules.
We illustrate it with the rule

be

\displaystyle C^{\prime}\cdot\theta\mathstrut

\mathit{PGInf}
inference

from

(See Definition

for the definition of
\mathcalx{J}^{-1}_{N}

The eligibility condition is fulfilled because the term order, and
the selections are transferred according to Definitions

and
12.1.3

and Lemma

The equality condition is fulfilled by Lemma

The conclusion

of this inference has the property

\mathcalx{J}(\mathit{concl}(\iota))=\mathit{concl}(\iota^{\prime})
, as desired.

Lemma 49

(Lifting of Order Conditions)
.

Let
t[\![T]\!]
and
s[\![S]\!]
be constrained terms over
\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{H}})
,
and let
\zeta
be a grounding substitution such that
S\zeta
and
T\zeta
are true.
If
t\zeta\succ s\zeta
, then
t[\![T]\!]\not\preceq s[\![S]\!]
.
The same holds for constrained literals.

Proof 12.11
.

We prove the contrapositive. If
t[\![T]\!]\preceq s[\![S]\!]
, then, by

(O7)
,

t\zeta\preceq s\zeta
.
Therefore, since
\succ
is asymmetric by
(O1)
,
t\zeta\not\succ s\zeta
.
The proof for constrained literals is analogous, using
(O6)

and
(O8)
.

Lemma 50

(Lifting of Maximality Conditions)
.

Let
C[\![S]\!]\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
.
Let
\theta
be a grounding substitution.
Let
L_{0}
be (strictly) maximal in
C\theta
.
Then there exists a literal
L
that is (strictly) maximal in
C[\![S]\!]

such that
L\theta=L_{0}
.

Proof 12.12
.

By Definition
4.4
, a literal
L
of a constrained clause
C[\![S]\!]
is maximal
if for all
K\in C
such that
K[\![S]\!]\succeq L[\![S]\!]
,
we have
K[\![S]\!]\preceq L[\![S]\!]
.

Since
L_{0}\in C\theta
, there exist literals
L
in
C[\![S]\!]
such that
L\theta=L_{0}
.
Let
L
be a maximal one among these literals.
A maximal one must exist because
\succ
is transitive on constrained literals by

(O9)

and transitivity implies existence of maximal elements in nonempty finite sets.
Let
K
be a literal in
C[\![S]\!]
such that
K[\![S]\!]\succeq L[\![S]\!]
.
We must show that
K[\![S]\!]\preceq L[\![S]\!]
.
By Lemma
49
,
K\theta\not\prec L\theta=L_{0}
.
By
(O1)
,
\succ
is a total order on ground terms, and thus
K\theta\succeq L_{0}
.
By maximality of
L_{0}
in
C\theta
, we have
K\theta\preceq L_{0}

and thus
K\theta=L_{0}
by
(O1)
.
Then
K[\![S]\!]\preceq L[\![S]\!]

because we chose
L
to be maximal among all literals in
C[\![S]\!]
such that
L\theta=L_{0}
.

For
strict
maximality, we simply observe that if
L
occurs more than once in
C

.

Lemma 51

(Lifting of Eligibility)
.

Let
N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{H}}
.

Let
C_{\mathrm{PG}}\cdot\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}\in\mathcalx{PG}(N)
,
let

.

–

Let

be a literal in

\mathcalx{PG}(\mathit{hsel},N)
.
Then there exists a literal

in
C_{\mathrm{H}}

such that

and

for all variables

in

,

L_{\mathrm{H}}
is (strictly) eligible in

w.r.t.

\sigma
and
\mathit{hsel}
.

–

Let
L_{\mathrm{PG}}.s_{\mathrm{PG}}.p_{\mathrm{PG}}
be a green position of
C_{\mathrm{PG}}\cdot\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}

that is eligible
w.r.t.

\mathcalx{PG}(\mathit{hsel},N)
.
Then there exists
a green position

of
C_{\mathrm{H}}

such that

–

L_{\mathrm{PG}}=L_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
;

–

s_{\mathrm{PG}}=s_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
;

–

*

p_{\mathrm{PG}}=p_{\mathrm{H}}
, or

*

for some nonempty

,
the subterm

at position
L_{\mathrm{H}}.s_{\mathrm{H}}.p_{\mathrm{H}}
of

is
not a variable but is

is nonfunctional; and

–

given substitutions
\sigma
and
\zeta
with
x\theta=x\sigma\zeta
for all variables

in

,

L_{\mathrm{H}}.s_{\mathrm{H}}.p_{\mathrm{H}}
is eligible in
C_{\mathrm{H}}[\![S]\!]

w.r.t.

\sigma
and
\mathit{hsel}
.

Proof 12.13
.

Let
L_{\mathrm{PG}}
be a literal in
C_{\mathrm{PG}}\cdot\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}
that is (strictly) eligible
w.r.t.

\mathcalx{PG}(\mathit{hsel},N)
.
By the definition of eligibility (Definition
9.3
),
there are two ways to be (strictly) eligible:

–

L_{\mathrm{PG}}
is selected by
\mathcalx{PG}(\mathit{hsel},N)
.
By Definition
12.1.4
,
there exists a literal
L_{\mathrm{H}}
selected by
\mathit{hsel}

such that
L_{\mathrm{PG}}=L_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.
By Definition
4.4
,
L_{\mathrm{H}}
is (strictly) eligible in

w.r.t.

\sigma

because it is selected.

–

There are no selected literals in

and

L_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}
is (strictly) maximal in
C_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}
.
By Definition
12.1.4
,
there are no selected literals in
C_{\mathrm{H}}[\![S]\!]
.
Since
C_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}=C_{\mathrm{H}}\theta=C_{\mathrm{H}}\sigma\zeta
,
by Lemma
50
,
there exists a literal

L_{\mathrm{H}}\in C_{\mathrm{H}}
such that
L_{\mathrm{H}}\sigma
is (strictly) maximal in

.
By Definition
4.4
,
L_{\mathrm{H}}
is (strictly) eligible in
C_{\mathrm{H}}[\![S]\!]

w.r.t.

\sigma
.

For the second part of the lemma,
let
L_{\mathrm{PG}}.s_{\mathrm{PG}}.p_{\mathrm{PG}}
be a green position of
C_{\mathrm{PG}}\cdot\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}

that is eligible
w.r.t.

\mathcalx{PG}(\mathit{hsel},N)
.
By Definition
9.3
,
the literal
L_{\mathrm{PG}}
is
of the form

with
s_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}\succ t_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}

and
L_{\mathrm{PG}}
is either
negative and
eligible
or positive and strictly eligible.
By the first part of this lemma,
there exists a literal
L_{\mathrm{H}}

in
C_{\mathrm{H}}
that is
either
negative and
eligible
or positive and strictly eligible in
C_{\mathrm{H}}[\![S]\!]

w.r.t.

\sigma
and
\mathit{hsel}
such that
L_{\mathrm{PG}}=L_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.
Then

must be of the form
s_{\mathrm{H}}\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}t_{\mathrm{H}}

with
s_{\mathrm{PG}}=s_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
and
t_{\mathrm{PG}}=t_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
.
Since
s_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}\succ t_{\mathrm{PG}}\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}
,
we have
s_{\mathrm{H}}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.8889pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\preceq}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.8889pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\preceq}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.125pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\preceq}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.70836pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\preceq}}}t_{\mathrm{H}}
.
By Definition
4.4
,
every green position in
L_{\mathrm{H}}.s_{\mathrm{H}}
is eligible
in
C_{\mathrm{H}}[\![S]\!]

w.r.t.

\sigma
and
\mathit{hsel}
.

It remains to show that there exists a green position
L_{\mathrm{H}}.s_{\mathrm{H}}.p_{\mathrm{H}}
in
C_{\mathrm{H}}
such that
either
p_{\mathrm{PG}}=p_{\mathrm{H}}
or

p_{\mathrm{PG}}=p_{\mathrm{H}}.q
for some nonempty
q
,
the subterm
u_{\mathrm{H}}
at position
L_{\mathrm{H}}.s_{\mathrm{H}}.p_{\mathrm{H}}
of
C_{\mathrm{H}}

is
not a variable but variable-headed,
and
u_{\mathrm{H}}\theta
is nonfunctional.

Since
p_{\mathrm{PG}}
is a green position of
s_{\mathrm{PG}}=s_{\mathrm{H}}\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
,
position
p_{\mathrm{PG}}
must either be a green position of
s_{\mathrm{H}}

or be below a variable-headed term in
s_{\mathrm{H}}
.
In the first case, we set

.
In the second case,
let
p_{\mathrm{H}}
be the position of the variable-headed term.
Then
p_{\mathrm{H}}.q=p_{\mathrm{PG}}
for some nonempty
q
.
Moreover, since
p_{\mathrm{PG}}
is a green position of
s_{\mathrm{PG}}
,
the subterm of
s_{\mathrm{PG}}
at position
p_{\mathrm{H}}
, which is
u_{\mathrm{H}}\theta
, cannot be functional.

Since
\mathfrak{p}(\theta)
maps nonfunctional variables to nonfunctional variables,
the subterm of
s_{\mathrm{H}}
at position
p_{\mathrm{H}}

cannot be a variable, but it is variable-headed.

Step (1) can be justified as follows: By Lemma
32
,

z_{\mathrm{H}}\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)\mathfrak{q}(\zeta)=v\theta_{\mathrm{PG}}
.
Since
z_{\mathrm{H}}\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)
and
v
contain only nonfunctional variables,

z_{\mathrm{H}}\sigma\mathfrak{p}(\zeta)
must be a
\lambda
-abstraction
whose
\lambda
binds exactly one De Bruijn index,
which is located at orange position
1.q

w.r.t.

\downarrow_{\beta\eta\mathrm{long}}
.
Thus,

12.2.
