In this subsection, we define a notion of trust for each level and connect them.
Ultimately, we prove that simple redundancy
({\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{C}}^{\star},{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}^{\star})

{defi}

.

Proof 12.15
.

Let
X
and
Y
the sets from Definition

.
We define a substitution
\rho^{\prime}

by
y\rho^{\prime}=y\rho{\downarrow_{R}}
for all variables

and

x\rho^{\prime}=x\rho
for all variables

.
By condition
2
of the definition of trust, we have

.
Moreover,

by

(
O2
)

PF

because

is oriented by
\succ
.

We show that

is also variable-irreducible.
If a variable

is in

, then

is reduced

R
by definition of
\rho^{\prime}
.
If a variable

is in

, then

in a literal

.
We must show that

is irreducible

the rules in

smaller than

.
By condition

,

in a literal

such that

is a subterm of

and

.
Since

is variable-irreducible

,

is irreducible

smaller than

.
Since

and

is a subterm of

, this implies that

is irreducible
w.r.t.
the rules in

smaller than

.

For the Boolean condition of variable-irreducibility,
we use that

’s only Boolean normal forms are

\top
\top

and
\bot

\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot

\bot
\bot

\bot

.

To show that

for all

12.2.2.
Indexed Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

In this subsubsection, let
\succ
be an admissible term order for
\mathit{IPGInf}
(Definition
10.0.1
).

The definition of trust is almost identical to the
corresponding definition on the
\mathrm{PF}{}
level.
However, we need to take into account that

\mathrm{PF}{}
level subterms correspond
to yellow subterms on the
\mathrm{IPG}{}

{defi}
[Trust]
A closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

trusts
a closure
D\cdot\rho\in N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
if the variables in
D
can be split into two sets
X
and
Y
such that

1.

for every literal

containing a variable

,
there exists a variable
z
in a literal
K\in C
such that
x\rho
is a yellow subterm of
z\theta
and
L\rho\preceq K\theta
; and

for all grounding substitutions
\rho^{\prime}
with
x\rho^{\prime}=x\rho
for all
x\not\in Y
,
we have
D\cdot\rho^{\prime}\in N
.

Lemma 54
.

If a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

w.r.t.

\succ
, then

trusts
\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho)\in\mathcalx{F}(N)

w.r.t.

\succ{F}
.

Proof 12.16
.

Assume

trusts
D\cdot\rho
. Thus, the variables of
D
can be split into two sets
X
and
Y
such that conditions
1
and
2
of the definition of trust are satisfied.
Note that the variables of
D
and
\mathcalx{F}(D)
coincide.
We claim that
\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)
trusts
\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho)
via the variable sets
X
and
Y
.

Let
\mathcalx{F}(L)\in\mathcalx{F}(D)
be a literal containing a variable
x\in X
.
Then
L\in D
contains
x
as well.
By the definition of trust (Definition
12.2.2
), there exists a variable
z
in some literal
K\in C
such that
x\rho
is a yellow subterm of
z\theta
and
L\rho\preceq K\theta
.
It holds that
\mathcalx{F}(L)\in\mathcalx{F}(D)
is a literal containing
x\in X
.
Since
x\rho
is a yellow subterm of

we have that
\mathcalx{F}(x\rho)
is a subterm of
\mathcalx{F}(z\theta)
.
Moreover, we have
\mathcalx{F}(L\rho)\preceq{F}\mathcalx{F}(K\theta)
.
Hence, condition

of Definition
12.2.1
is satisfied.

It remains to show that also condition

of Definition

that for any grounding substitution
\rho^{\prime}
with
x\rho^{\prime}=x\mathcalx{F}(\rho)
for all

, we have

\mathcalx{F}(D)\cdot\rho^{\prime}\in\mathcalx{F}(N)
.
We define a substitution

\rho^{\prime\prime}:x\mapsto\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(\rho^{\prime}(x))
.
Since
\mathcalx{F}^{-1}
maps ground terms to ground terms,

\rho^{\prime\prime}
is grounding.
Moreover,
since
\mathcalx{F}
is bijective on ground terms,

x\rho^{\prime\prime}=\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(\rho^{\prime}(x))=\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(x\mathcalx{F}(\rho))=x\rho
for all
x\not\in Y
.
By the definition of trust (Definition
12.2.2
),

D\cdot\rho^{\prime\prime}\in N

and therefore
\mathcalx{F}(D)\cdot\rho^{\prime}=\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho^{\prime\prime})\in\mathcalx{F}(N)
.

Lemma 55
.

Let
R
be a confluent term rewrite system on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
oriented by
\succ{F}
whose only Boolean normal forms are
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
\top
and
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
.
If a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
trusts a closure
D\cdot\rho\in N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

and
C\cdot\theta
is variable-irreducible, then
there exists a closure
D\cdot\rho^{\prime}\in\mathrm{irred}_{R}(N)

with
\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho^{\prime})\preceq{F}\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho)

such that
R\cup\{\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho^{\prime})\}\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho)
.

Proof 12.17
.

By Lemma

,

\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)
trusts
\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho)\in\mathcalx{F}(N)
.
By Lemma

,
there exists a closure

with
D_{0}\cdot\rho^{\prime}_{0}\preceq{F}\mathcalx{F}(D\cdot\rho)

such that

.
Thus, there must exist a closure

with

.

12.2.3.
Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

In this subsubsection, let
\succ
be an admissible term order for
\mathit{PGInf}
(Definition
11.0.1
).

As terms can also contain parameters we also need to account for this case in the definition of trust for the
\mathrm{PG}
level.
Specifically, we must add a condition that the variables
in

may not appear in parameters in the trusted closure.

{defi}

[Trust]
A closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}

trusts
a closure
D\cdot\rho\in N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
if the variables in
D
can be partitioned into two sets
X
and

such that

1.

for every literal
L\in D
containing a variable
x\in X
outside of parameters,
there exists a literal
K\in C
containing a variable
z
outside of parameters such that
x\rho
is a yellow subterm of
z\theta
and
L\rho\preceq K\theta
; and

all variables in
Y
do not appear in parameters in
D
and
for all grounding substitutions
\rho^{\prime}
with
x\rho^{\prime}=x\rho
for all
x\not\in Y
,

.

Lemma 56
.

If a closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}

Proof 12.18
.

Let

and

trusts

.

and

such that conditions

and

be the set

without the variables that only occur in parameters in

.
We claim that
\mathcalx{J}(C\cdot\theta)
trusts
\mathcalx{J}(D\cdot\rho)
using the sets

and

.

Since the parameters disappear after the application of the transformation
\mathcalx{J}

.

.
Since

is a yellow subterm of

is a yellow subterm of
\mathcalx{J}(z\theta)
, since

preserves yellow subterms.
Then, by Lemma

is a yellow subterm of

.
Moreover, we have
\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(K)\mathcalx{J}(\rho)=\mathcalx{J}(K\rho)\preceq{J}\mathcalx{J}(L\theta)=\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(L)\mathcalx{J}(\theta)
again using Lemma

Hence, condition

of Definition

Let
\rho^{\prime}
be a grounding substitution on the
\mathrm{IPG}

for all

.
Since

Since

is a grounding substitution

is a bijection on ground

.
This substitution

is grounding and

for all

.
Since
C\cdot\theta
trusts

, we have

and thus
\mathcalx{J}_{\rho^{\prime\prime}}(D)\cdot I(\rho^{\prime\prime})=\mathcalx{J}(D\cdot\rho^{\prime\prime})\in\mathcalx{J}(N)
.
Since the variables in
Y
do not occur in parameters in

,
we have
\mathcalx{J}_{\rho^{\prime\prime}}(D)=\mathcalx{J}_{\rho}(D)
.
Moreover,
\mathcalx{J}(\rho^{\prime\prime})=\rho^{\prime}
.
Hence, condition
2
of Definition
12.2.2
is satisfied.

Lemma 57
.

Let
R
be a confluent term rewrite system on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
oriented by

whose only Boolean normal forms are

12.3.
Model Construction

In this subsection,
we construct models of saturated clause sets,
starting with a first-order model and lifting it through the levels.
Using the results of Section
12.1
,
we prove a completeness property for each of the calculi
that roughly states
the following.
For any saturated set
N_{\infty}

that does not contain an empty closure,
there exists a term rewrite system
R
and a corresponding
interpretation
\mathscr{I}
such that
\mathscr{I}
is a model of the
closures in
N_{\infty}
that are variable-irreducible
w.r.t.

R
.

Moreover, to prepare the eventual extension the model of the variable-irreducible instances
to all instances, for each level,
we show a property that roughly states the following:
For any set of closures
N_{0}

that contains all closures
of the form
C\cdot\rho
for all
\rho
whenever it contains a closure
C\cdot\theta
,
then the variable-irreducible instances of
N_{0}
entail all of
N_{0}
.

Finally, in level
\mathrm{H}
,
we bring everything together by showing that the constructed model is
also a model
of the variable-irreducible ground instances
of
N_{0}
and thus of
N_{0}
itself.
It follows that the calculus
\mathit{HInf}
is refutationally complete.

12.3.1.

In this subsubsection, let
\succ
be an admissible term order for
\mathit{PFInf}
(Definition

and let

be a selection function on

(Definition

The completeness proof for
\mathit{PFInf}

relies on constructing a first-order term rewrite system.
For any first-order term rewrite system
R
, there exists
a first-order interpretation, which we also denote
R
, such that

R\models_{\mathrm{fol}}s\approx t
if and only if
s\leftrightarrow^{*}_{R}t
.
Formally, this can be implemented by
a first-order interpretation whose universe for each type
\tau
consists of
the
R
-equivalence classes of ground terms of type
\tau
.

{defi}

[
R_{N}
]

Lemma 62
.

The rewrite systems

and
R_{N}

do not have critical pairs and are oriented by
\succ
.

Proof 13.1
.

It is easy to check that all rules in

and
R_{N}
are oriented by
\succ
,
using

(
O4
)

PF

.

To show the absence of critical pairs, suppose that there exists a critical pair

and
s^{\prime}\rightarrow t^{\prime}
in

,
originating from
\Delta_{e}
and

e,e^{\prime}\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{F}}\cup\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{F}}
.
Without loss, we assume

.
Inspecting the rules of Definition
12.3.1
,
it follows that
s\succeq s^{\prime}
.

Lemma 64
.

For all ground clauses
C
, if
R_{C}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}C
, then
R_{N}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}C
.

Proof 13.3
.

We assume that
R_{C}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}C
.
Then we have
R_{C}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}L
for some literal
L
of
C
.
It suffices to show that
R_{N}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}L
.

If
L=t\approx t^{\prime}
is a positive literal,
then
t\leftrightarrow_{R_{C}}^{*}t^{\prime}
.
Since
R_{C}\subseteq R_{N}
,
this implies
t\leftrightarrow_{R_{N}}^{*}t^{\prime}
.
Thus,
R_{N}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}L
.

If
L=t\not\approx t^{\prime}
is a negative literal,
then
t\not\leftrightarrow_{R_{C}}^{*}t^{\prime}
.
By Lemma
62
,
this means that
t
and
t^{\prime}
have different normal forms
w.r.t.

R_{C}
.
Without loss of generality, let
t\succ t^{\prime}
. Let
s\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}s^{\prime}
be the maximal literal in
C
with
s\succeq s^{\prime}
.
We have
s\succ t
if
s\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}s^{\prime}
is positive and

s\succeq t
if
s\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}s^{\prime}
is negative.
Hence, inspecting Definition
12.3.1
,
we see that the left-hand sides of rules in
\bigcup_{e\succeq C}\Delta_{e}

are larger than
t
.
Since only rules with a left-hand side smaller or equal to
t
can be involved in normalizing
t
and
t^{\prime}

and
R_{C}\cup\bigcup_{e\succeq C}\Delta_{e}=R_{N}
,
it follows that
t
and
t^{\prime}
have different normal forms
w.r.t.

R_{N}
.
Therefore,
t\not\leftrightarrow_{R_{N}}^{*}t^{\prime}
and
R_{N}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}L
.

For

We employ a variant of Bachmair and Ganzinger’s
framework of reducing counterexamples
[
2
, Sect. 4.2]
.
Let

with
\bot\not\in\mathcalx{T}(N)
.
A closure

is called a

if
it is variable-irreducible w.r.t.
R_{N}
and

R_{N}\not\models_{\mathrm{fol}}C_{0}\cdot\theta
.
An inference

C_{0}\cdot\theta

C_{0}\cdot\theta
,
its side premises are in
N
and true in
R_{N}
, and
its conclusion is a counterexample smaller than
C_{0}\cdot\theta
.
An inference system has the
reduction property for counterexamples

if for all
N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PF}}
and all counterexamples
C_{0}\cdot\theta\in N
, there exists an inference from
N

that reduces
C_{0}\cdot\theta
.

Theorem 73
.

Let
N
be a set of closures that is saturated up to redundancy

w.r.t.

\mathit{PFInf}
and
\mathit{PFRed}_{\mathrm{I}}
,
and

N
does not contain

for any
\theta
.
Then
R_{N}\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathrm{irred}_{R_{N}}(N)
.

Proof 13.12
.

By Lemma
69
,
it suffices to show that
R_{N}\models_{\mathrm{fol}}\mathrm{irred}_{R_{N}}(N)
.
For a proof by contradiction,
we assume that
R_{N}\not\models_{\mathrm{fol}}\mathrm{irred}_{R_{N}}(N)
.
Then
N
contains a minimal counterexample, i.e.,
a closure
C_{0}\cdot\theta
that is variable-irreducible
w.r.t.

R_{N}

with

.
Since
\mathit{PFInf}
has the reduction property for counterexamples by Lemma
72
,
there exists an inference that reduces
C_{0}\cdot\theta
—i.e., an inference
\iota
with main premise
C_{0}\cdot\theta
,
side premises in
N
that are true in
R_{N}
,
and a conclusion

that is smaller than
C_{0}\cdot\theta,

variable-irreducible

R_{N}
, and false in
R_{N}
.
By saturation up to redundancy,

\iota\in\mathit{PFRed}_{\mathrm{I}}
.
By Definition
12.1.1
,
we have

R_{N}\cup\{E\in\mathrm{irred}_{R_{N}}(N)\mid E\prec C_{0}\cdot\theta\}\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathit{concl}(\iota)
.
By minimality of the counterexample
C_{0}\cdot\theta
,
the
closures
\{E\in\mathrm{irred}_{R_{N}}(N)\mid E\prec C_{0}\cdot\theta\}

must be true in
R_{N}
,
and it follows that
\mathit{concl}(\iota)
is true in

, a contradiction.

13.0.1.
Indexed Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

We write

for

, where

.

Our goal in this subsubsection is to use

to define a higher-order interpretation
that is a model of

.
To obtain a valid higher-order

in

.

Lemma 75

(Argument congruence)
.

Let
s\sim s^{\prime}
for
s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
.

.
Then
s\>u\sim s^{\prime}\>u
.

Proof 13.14
.

Let

be terms and

,

,

, and

are different variables.
Let
\rho
the substitution
resulting from

-normalizing all values of

(via

).
Then there exists the inference

IPGDiff

\displaystyle t\>{\mathsf{diff}}^{\tau,\upsilon}_{t\rho,t^{\prime}\rho}\not\approx t^{\prime}\>{\mathsf{diff}}^{\tau,\upsilon}_{t\rho,t^{\prime}\rho}\mathrel{\lor}t\>v\approx t^{\prime}\>v\cdot\rho\mathstrut

.

, its conclusion is variable-irreducible.

Since

.
Hence

by
Theorem
73

and
Lemma

.

We have
t\rho\sim t\theta=s\sim s^{\prime}=t^{\prime}\theta\sim t^{\prime}\rho
.

By

,

R\models\mathcalx{F}(t\rho\>{\mathsf{diff}}^{\tau,\upsilon}_{t\rho,t^{\prime}\rho})\approx\mathcalx{F}(t^{\prime}\rho\>{\mathsf{diff}}^{\tau,\upsilon}_{t\rho,t^{\prime}\rho})
.
Using Lemma

, it follows that

R\models\mathcalx{F}((t\>v\approx t^{\prime}\>v)\rho)
.

Since applying a functional term to an argument preserves nonfunctional yellow subterms of both
the functional term and its argument,
we have
s\>u=(t\>v)\theta\sim(t\>v)\rho
and

s^{\prime}\>u=(t^{\prime}\>v)\theta\sim(t^{\prime}\>v)\rho
.
So
R\models\mathcalx{F}(s\>u\approx s^{\prime}\>u)
and thus
s\>u\sim s^{\prime}\>u
.

The following lemma and its proof are essentially identical to
Lemma 54 of
Bentkamp et al.
[
6
]
.
We have adapted the proof to use De Bruijn indices,
and we have removed the notion of term-ground
and replaced it by preprocessing term variables,
which arguably would have been more elegant in the
original proof as well.

Lemma 76
.

Let
s\in\mathcalx{T}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
, and let
\theta
,
\theta^{\prime}
be grounding
substitutions such that
x\theta\sim x\theta^{\prime}
for all variables
x

and
\alpha\theta=\alpha\theta^{\prime}
for all type variables
\alpha
.
Then
s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
.

Proof 13.15
.

In this proof, we work directly on
\lambda
-terms. To prove the
lemma, it suffices to prove it
for any
\lambda
-term
s\in\mathcalx{T}^{\lambda}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
.
Here, for
t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathcalx{T}^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
, the notation

t_{1}\sim t_{2}
is to be read as
t_{1}\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta}\sim{t_{2}}\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta}

because
\mathcalx{F}
is defined only on
\beta
-normal
\lambda
-terms.

Without loss of generality, we may assume that
s
contains no type variables.
If
s
does contain type variables, we can instead use the term

s_{0}
resulting from instantiating each type variable
\alpha
in
s
with
\alpha\theta
.
If the result holds for the term
s_{0}
, which does not contain type variables, then

s_{0}\theta\sim s_{0}\theta^{\prime}
,
and thus the result also holds for
s
because
s\theta=s_{0}\theta

and
s\theta^{\prime}=s_{0}\theta^{\prime}
.

Definition
We extend the syntax of
\lambda
-terms with a new
polymorphic function symbol
\oplus:\mathsf{\Pi}\alpha.\;\alpha\rightarrow\alpha\rightarrow\alpha
.
We will omit its type argument. It is equipped with two reduction rules:

\oplus\>t\>s\rightarrow t
and
\oplus\>t\>s\rightarrow s
.
A
\beta\oplus
-reduction step

is either a rewrite step following one of these rules or a
\beta
-reduction step.

The computability path order
\succ_{\mathsf{CPO}}

[
12
]
guarantees that

–

\oplus\>t\>s\succ_{\mathsf{CPO}}s
by applying rule
@\rhd
;

–

\oplus\>t\>s\succ_{\mathsf{CPO}}t
by applying rule
@\rhd
twice;

–

(\lambda\>t)\>s\succ_{\mathsf{CPO}}t\{0\mapsto s\}
by applying rule
@\beta
.

Since this order is moreover monotone, it decreases with
\beta\oplus
-reduction steps.
The order is also well founded; thus,
\beta\oplus
-reductions terminate.
And since the
\beta\oplus
-reduction steps describe a finitely branching term rewriting
system, by Kőnig’s lemma
[
21
]
, there exists a maximal number of

\beta\oplus
-reduction steps
from each
\lambda
-term.

Definition
We introduce an auxiliary function
\mathscr{S}

that essentially measures the size of a
\lambda
-term but assigns a size of
1
to
ground
\lambda
-terms.

\mathscr{S}(s)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $s$ is ground or if $s$ is a variable}\\
1+\mathscr{S}(t)&\text{if $s$ is not ground and has the form $\lambda\>t$}\\
\mathscr{S}(t)+\mathscr{S}(u)&\text{if $s$ is not ground and has the form $t\>u$}\end{cases}

We prove
s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
by well-founded
induction on
s
,
\theta
, and
\theta^{\prime}
using
the left-to-right lexicographic order on the triple

\bigl(n_{1}(s),n_{2}(s),n_{3}(s)\bigr)\in\mathbb{N}^{4}
, where

–

n_{1}(s)
is the maximal number of

\beta\oplus
-reduction steps starting from
s\sigma
, where

\sigma
is the substitution mapping each variable
x

to
\oplus\>x\theta\>x\theta^{\prime}
;

–

n_{2}(s)
is the number of variables occurring more than once in
s
;

–

n_{3}(s)=\mathscr{S}(s)
.

Case 1:
The
\lambda
-term
s
is ground. Then the lemma is trivial.

Case 2:
The
\lambda
-term
s
contains
k\geq 2
variables. Then we can apply the induction
hypothesis twice and use the transitivity of
\sim
as follows. Let
x

be one of the variables in
s
. Let
\rho=\{x\mapsto x\theta\}
the
substitution that maps
x
to
x\theta
and ignores all other variables. Let

\rho^{\prime}=\theta^{\prime}[x\mapsto x]
.

We want to invoke the induction hypothesis on
s\rho
and
s\rho^{\prime}
.
This is justified because
s\sigma

\oplus
-reduces to
s\rho\sigma
and to

s\rho^{\prime}\sigma
, for
\sigma
as given in the definition of
n_{1}
.
These
\oplus
-reductions have at least one step because
x
occurs in
s
and
k\geq 2
.
Hence,
n_{1}(s)>n_{1}(s\rho)
and
n_{1}(s)>n_{1}(s\rho^{\prime})
.

This application of the induction hypothesis gives us

s\rho\theta\sim s\rho\theta^{\prime}
and
s\rho^{\prime}\theta\sim s\rho^{\prime}\theta^{\prime}
.
Since
s\rho\theta=s\theta
and
s\rho^{\prime}\theta^{\prime}=s\theta^{\prime}
,
this is equivalent to

s\theta\sim s\rho\theta^{\prime}
and
s\rho^{\prime}\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
.
Since moreover
s\rho\theta^{\prime}=s\rho^{\prime}\theta
, we have
s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
by
transitivity of
\sim
.
The following illustration visualizes the above argument:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s\rho}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s\rho^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s\theta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\scriptscriptstyle\text{IH}}{\sim}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s\rho\theta^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s\rho^{\prime}\theta}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underset{\scriptscriptstyle\text{IH}}{\sim}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s\theta^{\prime}}
\theta

\theta^{\prime}
\theta

\theta^{\prime}

Case 3:
The
\lambda
-term
s
contains a variable that occurs more than once. Then we rename
variable occurrences apart by replacing each occurrence of each variable
x
by
a fresh variable
x_{i}
, for which we define
x_{i}\theta=x\theta
and

x_{i}\theta^{\prime}=x\theta^{\prime}
. Let
s^{\prime}
be the resulting
\lambda
-term.
Since
s\sigma=s^{\prime}\sigma
for
\sigma
as given in the definition of
n_{1}
, we have
n_{1}(s)=n_{1}(s^{\prime})
. All variables occur only once in
s^{\prime}
.
Hence,
n_{2}(s)>0=n_{2}(s^{\prime})
. Therefore, we can invoke the induction
hypothesis on
s^{\prime}
to obtain
s^{\prime}\theta\sim s^{\prime}\theta^{\prime}
. Since
s\theta=s^{\prime}\theta
and
s\theta^{\prime}=s^{\prime}\theta^{\prime}
, it follows that

s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
.

Case 4:
The
\lambda
-term
s
contains only one variable
x
, which occurs exactly once.

Case 4.1:
The
\lambda
-term
s
is of the form
{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>\bar{t}

for some symbol
{\mathsf{f}}
, some types
\bar{\tau}
, and some

\lambda
-terms
\bar{t}
. Then let
u
be the
\lambda
-term in

\bar{t}
that contains
x
.
We want to apply the induction hypothesis to
u
, which can be
justified as follows.
For
\sigma
as given in the definition of
n_{1}
, consider the longest sequence of

\beta\oplus
-reductions from
u\sigma
. This sequence can be
replicated inside
s\sigma=({\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>\bar{t})\sigma
.
Therefore,
the longest sequence of
\beta\oplus
-reductions from
s\sigma
is at
least as long—i.e.,
n_{1}(s)\geq n_{1}(u)
. Since both
s
and
u
have
only one variable occurrence, we have
n_{2}(s)=0=n_{2}(u)
. But
n_{3}(s)>n_{3}(u)
because
u
is a nonground subterm of

s
.

Applying the induction hypothesis gives us
u\theta\sim u\theta^{\prime}
. By
definition of
\mathcalx{F}
, we have

\mathcalx{F}\!(({\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}\>\bar{t})\theta)={\mathsf{f}}_{m}^{\smash{\bar{\tau}}}\>\mathcalx{F}\!(\bar{t}\theta)

and analogously for
\theta^{\prime}
,
where
m
is the length of
\bar{t}
.
By congruence of
\approx
in first-order logic, it follows that
s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
.

Case 4.2:
The
\lambda
-term
s
is of the form
x\>\bar{t}
for some
\lambda
-terms
\bar{t}
. Then we
observe that, by assumption,
x\theta\sim x\theta^{\prime}
.
Since
x
occurs only once,

\bar{t}
are ground.
Then
x\theta\>\bar{t}\sim x\theta^{\prime}\>\bar{t}
by applying
Lemma
75
repeatedly.
Hence

s\theta=x\theta\>\bar{t}
and
s\theta=x\theta^{\prime}\>\bar{t}
,
and it follows that
s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
.

Case 4.3:
The
\lambda
-term
s
is of the form
\lambda\>u
for some
\lambda
-term
u
. Then we observe that to prove

s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
, by Lemma
68
, it suffices to show that

s\theta\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{s\theta,s\theta^{\prime}}\sim s\theta^{\prime}\>{\mathsf{diff}}_{s\theta,s\theta^{\prime}}
.
Via
\beta
-conversion, this is equivalent to

v\theta\sim v\theta^{\prime}
, where
v=u\{0\mapsto{\mathsf{diff}}_{s\theta,s\theta^{\prime}}\}
.
To prove
v\theta\sim v\theta^{\prime}
, we apply the
induction hypothesis on
v
.

It remains to show that the induction hypothesis applies on
v
.
For
\sigma
as given in the definition of
n_{1}
, consider the longest sequence of
\beta\oplus
-reductions from

v\sigma
. Since
{\mathsf{diff}}_{s\theta,s\theta^{\prime}}
is not a
\lambda
-abstraction, substituting it for
0

will not cause additional
\beta\oplus
-reductions. Hence, the same
sequence of
\beta\oplus
-reductions can be applied inside
s\sigma=(\lambda\>u)\sigma
, proving that
n_{1}(s)\geq n_{1}(v)
.
Since both
s
and
v
have only one variable occurrence,

n_{2}(s)=0=n_{2}(v)
. But
n_{3}(s)=\mathscr{S}(s)=1+\mathscr{S}(u)

because
s
is nonground. Moreover,

\mathscr{S}(u)=\mathscr{S}(v)=n_{3}(v)
. Hence,
n_{3}(s)>n_{3}(v)
, which justifies the application of the induction hypothesis.

Case 4.4:
The
\lambda
-term
s
is of the form
(\lambda\>u)\>t_{0}\>\bar{t}
for some
\lambda
-terms
u
,

t_{0}
, and
\bar{t}
.
We apply the induction hypothesis on
s^{\prime}=u\{0\mapsto t_{0}\}\>\bar{t}
,
justified as follows.
For
\sigma
as given in the definition of
n_{1}
, consider the longest sequence of
\beta\oplus
-reductions from

s^{\prime}\sigma
. Prepending the reduction
s\sigma\rightarrow_{\beta}s^{\prime}\sigma
to it gives us a longer sequence from
s\sigma
. Hence,

n_{1}(s)>n_{1}(s^{\prime})
.
The induction hypothesis gives us
s^{\prime}\theta\sim s^{\prime}\theta^{\prime}
. Since

\sim
is invariant under
\beta
-reductions, it follows that

s\theta\sim s\theta^{\prime}
.

Using the term rewrite system
R
,
we define a higher-order interpretation

\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}=(\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}},\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}_{\text{ty}},\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}},\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}})
.
The construction proceeds as in
the completeness proof of the original
\lambda
-superposition calculus
[
6
]
.
Let
(\mathscr{U},\mathscr{J})=R
; i.e.,
\mathscr{U}_{\tau}
is the universe for the first-order type
\tau
, and
\mathscr{J}
is the interpretation function.
Since the higher-order and first-order type signatures are identical, we can identify ground higher-order and first-order types.
We will define a domain
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
for each ground type
\tau
and then let
\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
be the set of all these domains
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
.
We cannot identify the domains
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
with the first-order domains
\mathscr{U}_{\tau}

because domains
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
for functional types
\tau
must contain functions.
Instead, we will define suitable domains
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
and a bijection
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
between
\mathscr{U}_{\tau}
and
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
for each ground type
\tau
.

We define
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
and
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
in mutual recursion.
To ensure well definedness, we must show that
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
is bijective.
We start with nonfunctional types
\tau
:
Let
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}=\mathscr{U}_{\tau}
, and let
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}:\mathscr{U}_{\tau}\to\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
be the identity.
Clearly, the identity is bijective.
For functional types, we define

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{\tau\to\upsilon}=\{\varphi:\mathscr{D}_{\tau}\to\mathscr{D}_{\upsilon}\mid\exists s:\tau\to\upsilon.\ \forall u:\tau.\ \varphi\left(\mathscr{E}_{\tau}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(u)\rrbracket_{R}})\right)=\mathscr{E}_{\upsilon}\left(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s\>u)\rrbracket_{R}}\right)\}

\displaystyle\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}:\mathscr{U}_{\tau\to\upsilon}\to\mathscr{D}_{\tau\to\upsilon}

\displaystyle\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}})\left(\mathscr{E}_{\tau}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(u)\rrbracket_{R}})\right)=\mathscr{E}_{\upsilon}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s\>u)\rrbracket_{R}})

To verify that this equation is a valid definition of
\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
, we must show that

–

every element of
\mathscr{U}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
is of the form
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}}
for some
s\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
;

–

every element of
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}
is of the form
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}\left(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(u)\rrbracket_{R}}\right)
for some
u\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
;

–

the definition does not depend on the choice of such
s
and
u
; and

–

\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}})\in\mathscr{D}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
for all
s\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
.

The first claim holds because
R
is term-generated and
\mathcalx{F}
is a bijection.
The second claim holds because
R
is term-generated and
\mathcalx{F}
and
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
are bijections.
To prove the third claim, we assume that there are other terms
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
and
v\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
such that
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t)\rrbracket_{R}}
and
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}\left(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(u)\rrbracket_{R}}\right)=\mathscr{E}_{\tau}\left(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(v)\rrbracket_{R}}\right)
.
Since
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
is bijective, we have
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(u)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(v)\rrbracket_{R}}
—i.e.,
u\sim v
.
The terms
s,t,u,v
are in
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
, allowing us to apply Lemma
76

to the term
x\>y
and the substitutions
\{x\mapsto s{,}\;y\mapsto u\}
and
\{x\mapsto t{,}\;y\mapsto v\}
.
Thus, we obtain
s\>u\sim t\>v
—i.e.,
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s\>u)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t\>v)\rrbracket_{R}}
—indicating that the definition of
\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
above does not depend on the choice of
s
and
u
.
The fourth claim is obvious from the definition of
\mathscr{D}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
and the third claim.

It remains to show that
\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
is bijective.
For injectivity, we fix two terms
s,t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
such that for all
u\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
, we have
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s\>u)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t\>u)\rrbracket_{R}}
.
By Lemma
68
, it follows that
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t)\rrbracket_{R}}
, which shows that
\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
is injective.
For surjectivity, we fix an element
\varphi\in\mathscr{D}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
.
By definition of
\mathscr{D}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
, there exists a term
s
such that
\varphi\left(\mathscr{E}_{\tau}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(u)\rrbracket_{R}})\right)=\mathscr{E}_{\upsilon}\left(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s\>u)\rrbracket_{R}}\right)
for all
u
.
Hence,
\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}})=\varphi
, proving surjectivity and therefore bijectivity of
\mathscr{E}_{\tau\to\upsilon}
.
Below, we will usually write
\mathscr{E}
instead of
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
since the type
\tau
is determined by
\mathscr{E}_{\tau}
’s first argument.

We define the higher-order universe as
\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}}=\{\mathscr{D}_{\tau}\mid\tau\text{ ground}\}
.
In particular, by Lemma
69
, this implies that
\mathscr{D}_{o}=\{0,1\}\in\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
as needed, where

is identified with

Moreover, we define
\mathscr{J}_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\kappa)(\mathscr{D}_{\bar{\tau}})=\mathscr{D}_{\kappa(\bar{\tau})}
for all

,
completing the type interpretation of

We define the interpretation function
\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
for symbols

\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}({\mathsf{f}},\mathscr{D}_{\bar{\upsilon}_{m}})=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}({\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\upsilon}_{m}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt})\rrbracket_{R}})

We must show that this definition indeed fulfills the requirements of an interpretation function.
By definition, we have

(I1)

\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\kern 0.17224pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\top$}\kern-7.7778pt\raise (I7)

Let
\mathscr{D}_{\tau}\in\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
and

.

which is

.

(I8)
Similarly
\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\mathrel{\kern 0.17224pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\kern-0.08612pt\raise 0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise 0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.08612pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern-18.05551pt\raise-0.17224pt\hbox{$\not\approx$}\kern 0.17224pt},\mathscr{D}_{\tau})(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})=0
if
a^{\prime}=b^{\prime}
and
1
otherwise.
This concludes the proof that
\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is an interpretation function.

Finally, we need to define the designation function
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
, which takes a valuation
\xi
and a
\lambda
-expression as arguments.
Given a valuation
\xi
, we choose a grounding substitution
\theta
such that
\mathscr{D}_{\alpha\theta}=\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}(\alpha)
and
\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(x\theta)\rrbracket_{R}})=\xi_{\mathsf{te}}(x)
for all type variables
\alpha
and all variables
x
.
Such a substitution can be constructed as follows: We can fulfill the first equation in a unique way because there is a one-to-one correspondence between ground types and domains.
Since
\mathscr{E}^{-1}(\xi_{\mathsf{te}}(x))
is an element of a first-order universe and
R
is term-generated, there exists a ground term
s
such that
\smash{\llbracket s\rrbracket_{R}^{\xi}}=\mathscr{E}^{-1}(\xi_{\mathsf{te}}(x))
.
Choosing one such
s
and defining
x\theta=\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(s)
gives us a grounding substitution
\theta
with the desired property.

Let
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\xi,\lambda\>t)=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}((\lambda\>t)\theta)\rrbracket_{R}})
.
We need to show that our definition does not depend on the choice of
\theta
.
We assume that there exists another substitution
\theta^{\prime}
with the properties
\mathscr{D}_{\alpha\theta^{\prime}}=\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}(\alpha)
for all
\alpha
and
\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(x\theta^{\prime})\rrbracket_{R}})=\xi_{\mathsf{te}}(x)
for all
x
.
Then we have
\alpha\theta=\alpha\theta^{\prime}
for all
\alpha
due to the one-to-one correspondence between domains and ground types.
We have
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(x\theta)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(x\theta^{\prime})\rrbracket_{R}}
for all
x
because
\mathscr{E}
is injective.
By Lemma
76
it follows that
\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}((\lambda\>t)\theta)\rrbracket_{R}}=\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}((\lambda\>t)\theta^{\prime})\rrbracket_{R}}
, which proves that
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is well defined.
This concludes the definition of the interpretation
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}=(\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}},\mathscr{J}_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\mathrm{IPG}},\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}},\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}})
.
It remains to show that
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is proper.

The higher-order interpretation
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
relates to the first-order
interpretation
R
as follows:

Lemma 77
.

Given a ground
\lambda
-term
t\in\mathcalx{T}^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
, we have

\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

Proof 13.16
.

The proof is adapted from the proof of Lemma 40 in Bentkamp et al.
[
8
]
.
We proceed by induction on
t
.
If
t
is of the form
{\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}
, then

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}

\displaystyle=\mathscr{J}^{\mathrm{IPG}}({\mathsf{f}},\mathscr{D}_{\bar{\tau}})

\displaystyle=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!({\mathsf{f}}{\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle\kern-0.83328pt})\rrbracket_{R}})=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!(t\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

If
t
is an application
t=t_{1}\>t_{2}
, where
t_{1}
is of type
\tau\rightarrow\upsilon
, then

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket t_{1}\>t_{2}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket t_{1}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}(\smash{\llbracket t_{2}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}})

\displaystyle\overset{\!\scriptscriptstyle\text{IH}\!}{=}\mathscr{E}_{\tau\rightarrow\upsilon}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!(t_{1}\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})(\mathscr{E}_{\tau}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!(t_{2}\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}}))

\displaystyle\overset{\kern-28.45274pt\text{Def }\mathscr{E}\kern-28.45274pt}{=}\enskip\mathscr{E}_{\upsilon}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((t_{1}\>t_{2})\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

If
t
is a
\lambda
-expression, then

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket\lambda\>u\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\xi,\lambda\>u)

\displaystyle=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((\lambda\>u)\theta\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

\displaystyle=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((\lambda\>u)\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

where
\theta

is a substitution as required by the definition of
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
.

We need to show that the interpretation
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is
proper. In the proof, we will need the following lemma, which is
very similar to the substitution lemma (Lemma
22
),
but we
must prove it here for our particular interpretation
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
because we have not
shown that
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is proper yet.

Lemma 78
.

Let
\rho
be a grounding substitution,
t
be a
\lambda
-term, and
\xi
be a valuation.
Moreover, we define a valuation
\xi^{\prime}
by
\vphantom{(_{(_{(}}}\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime}(\alpha)=\smash{\llbracket\alpha\rho\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}}}
for all type variables
\alpha
and
\xi_{\mathsf{te}}^{\prime}(x)=\smash{\llbracket x\rho\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi}}
for all term variables
x
.
We then have

\smash{\llbracket t\rho\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi}}=\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}

Proof 13.17
.

The proof is adapted from the proof of Lemma 41 in Bentkamp et al.
[
8
]
.
We proceed by induction on the structure of
\tau
and
t
.
The proof is identical to that of Lemma
22
,
except for the last case, which uses properness of the interpretation, a
property we cannot assume here.
However, here, we have the assumption that
\rho
is a grounding substitution.
Therefore, if
t
is a
\lambda
-expression, we argue as follows:

\displaystyle\smash{\llbracket(\lambda\>u)\rho\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket\lambda\>u\rho\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi}}

\displaystyle=\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\xi,\lambda\>u\rho)

by the definition of the term denotation

\displaystyle=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((\lambda\>u)\rho\theta\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

for some
\theta
by the definition of
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}

\displaystyle=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((\lambda\>u)\rho\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

because
(\lambda\>u)\rho
is ground

\displaystyle\overset{\smash{*}}{=}\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\xi^{\prime},\lambda\>u)

by the definition of
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
and Lemma
77

\displaystyle=\smash{\llbracket\lambda\>u\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{\xi^{\prime}}}

by the definition of the term denotation

The step labeled with
*
is justified as follows:
We have

\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\xi^{\prime},\lambda\>u)=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((\lambda\>u)\theta^{\prime}\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

by the definition of
\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
,
if
\theta^{\prime}
is a substitution such that

\smash{\mathscr{D}_{\alpha\theta^{\prime}}}=\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime}(\alpha)
for all
\alpha
and

\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!(x\theta^{\prime}\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})=\xi_{\mathsf{te}}^{\prime}(x)

for all
x
.
By the definition of
\xi^{\prime}
and by Lemma
77
,

\rho
is such a substitution.
Hence,

\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}(\xi^{\prime},\lambda\>u)=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}\!((\lambda\>u)\rho\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})
.

Lemma 79
.

The interpretation
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is proper.

Proof 13.18
.

We need to show that
\smash{\llbracket\lambda\>t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}})}}(a)=\smash{\llbracket t\{0\mapsto x\}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}}[x\mapsto a])}}
, where
x
is a fresh variable.

\begin{array}[]{rll}\smash{\llbracket\lambda\>t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}})}}(a)&=\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}((\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}}),\lambda\>t)(a)&\text{by the definition of term denotation}\\[3.0pt]
&=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}((\lambda\>t)\theta\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})(a)&\text{by the definition of $\mathscr{L}^{\mathrm{IPG}}$ for some $\theta$}\\
&&\text{such that $\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(z\theta)\rrbracket_{R}})=\xi_{\mathsf{te}}(z)$ for}\\
&&\text{all $z$ and $\mathscr{D}_{\alpha\theta}=\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha$}\\[3.0pt]
&=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(((\lambda\>t)\theta\>s)\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})&\text{by the definition of $\mathscr{E}$}\\
&&\text{where $\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(s)\rrbracket_{R}})=a$}\\[3.0pt]
&=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t\{0\mapsto x\}(\theta[x\mapsto s])\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})&\text{by $\beta$-reduction}\\
&&\text{where $x$ is fresh}\\[3.0pt]
&=\smash{\llbracket t\{0\mapsto x\}(\theta[x\mapsto s])\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}&\text{by Lemma \ref{lem:IPG:ho-fo-correspondence}}\\[3.0pt]
&=\smash{\llbracket t\{0\mapsto x\}\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}^{(\xi_{\mathsf{ty}},\xi_{\mathsf{te}}[x\mapsto a])}}&\text{by Lemma \ref{lem:IPG:interpretation-substitution}}\end{array}

Lemma 80
.

\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is term-generated; i.e.,
for all
\mathscr{D}\in\mathscr{U}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
and all
a\in\mathscr{D}
,
there exists a ground type
\tau
such that

\smash{\llbracket\tau\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=\mathscr{D}
and
a ground term
t
such that

\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=a
.

Proof 13.19
.

In the construction above, it is clear that there is a one-to-one
correspondence between ground types and domains, which yields a suitable
ground type
\tau
.

Since
R
is term-generated, there must be a ground term
s\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
such
that
\smash{\llbracket s\rrbracket_{R}}=\mathscr{E}^{-1}(a)
.
Let
t=\mathcalx{F}^{-1}(s)
.
Then, by Lemma
77
,

\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket s\rrbracket_{R}})=a
.

Lemma 81
.

Given
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
,
we have
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models C\cdot\theta
if and only if

R\models\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)
.

Proof 13.20
.

By Lemma
77
,
we have

\smash{\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=\mathscr{E}(\smash{\llbracket\mathcalx{F}(t\kern 0.83328pt{\downarrow}_{\beta})\rrbracket_{R}})

for any
t\in\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{ground}}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{I}})
.
Since
\mathscr{E}
is a bijection,
it follows that a ground literal

s\theta\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}t\theta
in a clause
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}

is true in
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
if and only if

\mathcalx{F}(s\theta\mathrel{\dot{\approx}}t\theta)
is true in
R
.
So any closure
C\cdot\theta\in\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
is
true in
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
if and only if

\mathcalx{F}(C\cdot\theta)
is true in
R
.

Theorem 82
.

Let
N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
be saturated up to redundancy
w.r.t.

\mathit{IPGRed}_{\mathrm{I}}
,
and

N
does not contain a closure of the form
\bot\cdot\theta
for any
\theta
.
Then
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathrm{irred}_{R}({N})
, where
R=R_{\mathcalx{F}(N)}
.

Proof 13.21
.

By Lemma
81
, it suffices to show that
R
is a model of

\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{F}(N))
.
We apply Theorem
73
.
Lemma
43
shows the condition of saturation up to redundancy.

.

can be derived from this lemma’s condition on

and the fact that
\mathcalx{F}
is a bijection (Lemma
25
).

13.0.2.
Partly Substituted Ground Higher-Order Level

In this subsubsection,
let
\succ
be an admissible term order for
\mathit{PGInf}
(Definition
11.0.1
),
and let
\mathit{pgsel}
be a selection function on
\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
(Definition
9.3
).

It is inconvenient to construct a model of
N_{0}
for the
\mathrm{PG}
level
because
\mathcalx{J}
converts parameters into subscripts.
For example, in the model constructed in the previous subsubsection,
it can happen that
{\mathsf{a}}\approx{\mathsf{b}}
holds,
but
{\mathsf{f}}_{\mathsf{a}}\approx{\mathsf{f}}_{\mathsf{b}}
does not hold,
where
{\mathsf{a}}
and
{\mathsf{b}}
are constants
and
{\mathsf{f}}_{\mathsf{a}}
and
{\mathsf{f}}_{\mathsf{b}}
are constants originating
from a constant
{\mathsf{f}}
with a parameter.
For this reason, our completeness result for the
\mathrm{PG}
level
only constructs a model of
\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{J}(N))\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{IPG}}
instead of
\mathrm{irred}_{R}(N)\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
.
We will overcome this flaw when we lift the result to the
\mathrm{H}
level
where the initial clause set can be assumed not to contain any constants with parameters.

Theorem 84
.

Let
N\subseteq\mathcalx{C}_{\mathrm{PG}}
be saturated up to redundancy
w.r.t.

\mathit{PGRed}_{\mathrm{I}}
,
and

N
does not contain a closure of the form
\bot\cdot\theta
for any
\theta
.
Then
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathcalx{J}(\mathrm{irred}_{R}(N))
, where
R=R_{\mathcalx{F}(\mathcalx{J}(N))}
.

Proof 13.23
.

This follows from
Theorem
82

and Lemma
46
.

Lemma 85
.

Let
R
be a confluent term rewrite system on
\mathcalx{T}_{\mathrm{PF}}
oriented by
\succ_{\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{F}}

whose only Boolean normal forms are
\top
\top
\top
\top

and
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot

\bot
\bot

\bot
\bot
\bot
\bot

.
Let

such that for every

that

on all variables not occurring in

Proof 13.24
.

We apply Lemma
83
.
The required condition on
\mathcalx{J}(N)

can be derived from this lemma’s condition on

as follows.
We must show that
for every

and every grounding substitution
\rho
that
coincides with

The closure

\mathcalx{J}(C^{\prime}\cdot\theta^{\prime})

with

.
Define

as

for all

By this lemma’s condition on

,

and thus

Here, it is crucial that

does not contain parameters because only this guarantees

.

13.0.3.
Full Higher-Order Level

In this subsubsection, let
\succ

(Definition

{defi}

A
derivation
is a finite or infinite sequence of sets
(N_{i})_{i\geq 0}

such that

for all

A derivation is called

\mathit{HInf}
-inferences from clauses in
\bigcup_{i}\bigcap_{j\geq i}N_{j}

are contained in
\bigcup_{i}{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}(N_{i})
.

Lemma 86
.

The redundancy criteria
{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{C}}
and

fulfill the following properties,
as stated by Waldmann et al.
[

]
:

(R2)

, then

{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}(N)\subseteq{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}(N^{\prime})

(R3)

{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{C}}(N)\subseteq{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{C}}(N\setminus N^{\prime})

and
{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}(N)\subseteq{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}(N\setminus N^{\prime})
;

(R4)

if

and
\mathit{concl}(\iota)\in N
, then
\iota\in HRedI(N)
.

.

(R2): This is obvious by definition of clause and inference redundancy.

(R3) for clauses:

if and only if for

Theorem 88
.

Given a fair derivation

(N_{i})_{i\geq 0}
, where

1.

N_{0}
does not have a term-generated model,

2.

N_{0}
does not contain parameters, and

3.

N_{0}
does not contain constraints,

we have
\bot[\![S]\!]\in N_{i}
for some satisfiable constraints
S
and some index
i
.

Proof 13.27
.

By Lemma 9 of Waldmann et al.
[
33
]
,
using Lemma
86
,
the limit
N_{\infty}=\bigcup_{i}\bigcap_{j\geq i}N_{j}

is saturated up to redundancy
w.r.t.

\mathit{HInf}
and
{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{I}}
.
By Lemma
52
,

\mathcalx{PG}(N_{\infty})
is saturated up to redundancy

w.r.t.

\mathit{PGInf}
and
\mathit{PGRed}_{\mathrm{I}}
.

For a proof by contradiction,
assume that for
all
S
and
all
i
,

\bot[\![S]\!]\not\in N_{i}
.
Then
N_{\infty}
does not contain such a clause
\bot[\![S]\!]
either,
and thus
\mathcalx{PG}(N_{\infty})
does not contain a clause of the form
\bot\cdot\theta
for any
\theta
.
By
Lemma
84
,

\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{J}(\mathcalx{PG}(N_{\infty})))
, where
R=R_{\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{\infty})}
.

By Lemma 8 of Waldmann et al.
[
33
]
,
using Lemma
86
,

N_{0}\subseteq N_{\infty}\cup{\mathit{HRed}}_{\mathrm{C}}(N_{\infty})
.
Thus,

R\cup\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{\infty}))\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{0}))
.
By Lemma
87
and
conditions
2
and
3
from the present
theorem,

R\cup\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{0}))\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{0})

and thus
R\cup\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{\infty}))\models_{\mathrm{o\lambda}}\mathcalx{F}\mathcalx{J}\mathcalx{P}\mathcalx{G}(N_{0})
.

Since

\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathrm{irred}_{R}(\mathcalx{J}(\mathcalx{PG}(N_{\infty})))
,
by Lemma
81
,
it follows that

\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathcalx{J}(\mathcalx{P}(\mathcalx{G}(N_{0})))
.

If we applied each closure’s substitution to its clause in the sets

\mathcalx{J}(\mathcalx{P}(\mathcalx{G}(N_{0})))
and
\mathcalx{J}({\mathsf{Gnd}}(N_{0}))
,
the two sets would be identical.
So, since

\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathcalx{J}(\mathcalx{P}(\mathcalx{G}(N_{0})))
,
we have
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models\mathcalx{J}({\mathsf{Gnd}}(N_{0}))
.

Now
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
can be shown to be a model of
N_{0}
as follows.
Let
C\in N_{0}
. Let
\xi
be a valuation. Since
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
is term-generated by Lemma
80
,
there exists a substitution
\theta
such that
\smash{\llbracket\alpha\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}(\alpha)

for all type variables
\alpha
in
C
and
\smash{\llbracket x\theta\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}}}=\xi_{\mathsf{te}}(x)
for all term variables
x
in
C
.
Since
C
does not contain parameters by condition
2
of this theorem,

C\theta\in\mathcalx{J}({\mathsf{Gnd}}(N_{0}))
. Thus we have
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models C\theta
.
By Lemma
23
, it follows that
C
is true
w.r.t.

\xi
and
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}
.
Since
\xi
and
C\in N_{0}
were arbitrary, we have
\mathscr{I}^{\mathrm{IPG}}\models N_{0}
.
This contradicts condition
1
of the present theorem.

{\mathsf{diff}}
-aware model
\mathscr{I}^{\prime}=(\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}^{\prime},\mathscr{J}^{\prime},\mathscr{L}^{\prime})
as follows.

We define
\mathscr{J}^{\prime}({\mathsf{diff}},\mathscr{D}_{1},\mathscr{D}_{2},a,b)

to be an element
e\in\mathscr{D}_{1}
such that

a(e)\neq b(e)
if such an element exists and an arbitrary element of
\mathscr{D}_{1}
otherwise.
This ensures that
\mathscr{I}^{\prime}
is
{\mathsf{diff}}
-aware (Definition
3.1
).

To define
\mathscr{L}^{\prime}
, let
\xi
be a valuation and
t
be a
\lambda
-abstraction.
We replace each occurrence of
{\mathsf{diff}}{\langle\tau,\upsilon\rangle\kern-0.83328pt}(u,w)
in
t

with a ground term
s
that does not contain
{\mathsf{diff}}
such that

\smash{\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}}=\mathscr{J}^{\prime}({\mathsf{diff}},\smash{\llbracket\tau\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}}},\smash{\llbracket\upsilon\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}_{\mathsf{ty}}}^{\xi_{\mathsf{ty}}}},\smash{\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}},\smash{\llbracket w\rrbracket_{\mathscr{I}}^{\xi}})
.
Such a term
s
exists because
\mathscr{I}
is term-generated.
We start replacing the innermost occurrences of
{\mathsf{diff}}
and proceed outward
to ensure that the parameters of a replaced
{\mathsf{diff}}
do not contain
{\mathsf{diff}}
themselves.
Let
t^{\prime}
be the result of this replacement.
Then we define
\mathscr{L}^{\prime}(\xi,t)=\mathscr{L}(\xi,t^{\prime})
.
This ensures that
\mathscr{I}^{\prime}
is a proper interpretation.

Since
N
does not contain
{\mathsf{diff}}

and
\mathscr{I}
is a model of
N
,
it follows that
\mathscr{I}^{\prime}
is a model of
N
as well.

Corollary 90
.

Given a fair derivation

(N_{i})_{i\geq 0}
, where

1.

N_{0}\mathrel{|\kern-0.43057pt}\joinrel\approx\bot
,

2.

N_{0}
does not contain parameters, and

3.

N_{0}
does not contain constraints,

we have
\bot[\![S]\!]\in N_{i}
for some satisfiable constraints
S
and some index
i
.

Proof 13.29
.

By Theorem
88
and Lemma
89
.

14.
Conclusion

We presented the optimistic
\lambda
-superposition calculus. It is inspired by
the original
\lambda
-superposition calculus of Bentkamp et
al.
[
6
]
, which in turn generalizes the
standard superposition calculus by Bachmair and Ganzinger

[
1
]
.
Our calculus has many advantages over the original
\lambda
-superposition
calculus, including more efficient handling of unification, functional
extensionality, and redundancy. Admittedly, its main disadvantage is its
lengthy refutational completeness proof.

We have some ideas on how to extend the calculus further:

–

We believe that the inference rules that still require full unification
could be adapted to work with partial unification by adding annotations to constrained clauses.
The annotations would indicate which variables and which constraints stem from
rules with the
Fluid
- prefix.
A modification of the map
\mathfrak{p}
used in our proof could ensure that these variables
do not carry the guarantee of being variable-irreducible that currently all variables carry.
As a result, the proof of Lemma
52
would
no longer require full unification,
but additional
FluidSup
inferences would be required into the variables
marked by the annotations.

–

We conjecture that the
Diff
axiom is not necessary for
refutational completeness although our proof
currently requires it.
Our proof uses it in Lemma
75
to show that the constructed model
is a valid higher-order model in the sense that
equality of functions
implies equality of their values on all arguments.
We suspect that one can construct a
model with this property using saturation
w.r.t.

ArgCong
alone,
but the model construction must be different from the one used in the present proof.

–

One of the most explosive rules of the calculus is
FluidSup
.
Bhayat and Suda
[
11
]
propose
a modification of inference rules
that delays flex-rigid pairs and flex-flex pairs by adding
them as negative literals to the conclusion.
They suggest that this modification in conjunction
with additional inference rules for the unification of
flex-rigid pairs could remove the need for
FluidSup
.
We conjecture that one could prove refutational completeness of such a calculus
by restructuring Lemma
72

to apply the modified inference rules
instead of Lemma
71
whenever
the only terms reducible by
R_{C}

correspond to positions below applied variables on level
\mathrm{H}
.

–

Similarly,
we conjecture that one could remove the
Ext
rule
by following the idea of Bhayat
[
10
]
to
delay unification of functional terms
by adding them as negative literals to the conclusion.
If we immediately apply
NegExt
to these additional literals,
one can possibly prove refutational completeness
by restructuring Lemma
72

to apply the modified inference rules
instead of Lemma
71
whenever
the only terms reducible by
R_{C}
are functional terms.
